tahyatiriktatvaṃ guṇālaṅkāravyatiriktatvam /
vṛttīnāntāvadanuprāsālaṅkārāntarbhāvaṃ darśayitumāha--tathā hyanuprāsānāmevetyādi /
anuprāsānāmevetyasya vargatrayasampādanārthamityanena sambandhaḥ /
tadapi kimarthamityātrāha--paruṣatvetyādi /
paruṣatvādisvarūpāṇāṃ viśiṣya pradarśanārthamityarthaḥ /
tasyāpi phalamāha--dīpteti /
dīptaṃ raudrādaurase, masṛṇaṃ madhuraṃ śṛṅgarādau, madhyamaṃ hāsyādau, tathāvidhaṃ yadvarṇanīyaṃ vibhāvādi, tadupayogityā varṇanīyaviśeṣopayogitvenānuprasaviśeṣopādeyatāsiddhyarthamityarthaḥ /
anuprāsajātaya iti /
anuprāsānāmāśrayabhūtā jātaya ityārthaḥ /
vivariṣyate cedamupari. vṛttaya ityuktāḥ vṛttaya iti vyavahṛtāḥ /
tatra vyutpattimāha--vartanta iti /
anuprāsabhedāḥ anuprāsaviśeṣāḥ /
āsviti /
vṛttirityatra vṛtidhātoradhikaraṇe ktinniti bhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: As he says 'yadā' ('when') —
<s>Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa</s> — this is to be supplied.
As [he says] 'sarūpā' ('of the same form') —
Among these, poets always employ the <s>Locana</s> (eye/commentary) separately for each [type of] <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliterative ornamentation).

The <s>Bālapriyā</s> [explains]: 'what is about to be stated' — by means of '<s>ācakṣīran</s>' etc., 'what will be stated.' 'To establish' — the meaning is: to prove by the universal rule (<s>vyāpti</s>) that 'whatever exists can be supposed.' '[The vṛttikāra] says "<s>sambhavantī</s>"' — the meaning is: he says [the passage] from '<s>tadabhāvavādinām</s>' up to '<s>sambhavantī</s>.' Now, if in place of '<s>sambhavantī</s>' one were to say '<s>sambhāvyante</s>,' then the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>) would already have been made at the outset — to this he says: '<s>sambhāvyante</s>' etc. 'Of repeated meaning' — the meaning is: 'by the optative forms (<s>liṅ</s>).' Now, should the existence (<s>sambhava</s>) that is the root of the supposition also be supposed? No — he says '<s>na ca</s>' etc. 'By the present [tense]' — the meaning is: 'by <s>laṭ</s> (present tense).' He introduces what was stated as '<s>vikalpāḥ</s>' (alternatives) — '<s>nanu ca</s>' etc. '[A supposition] whose support is the substratum of an existent real entity' — [where] '<s>sambhāvita</s>' means 'made the object of, or produced.' [The objection:] 'How is the refutation [achieved] merely by saying "<s>vikalpāḥ</s>"?' — to this he explains the manner: '<s>na tu</s>' etc. '<s>Tāddak</s>-supposition' — the supposed real entity does not exist in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārtha</s>). The reason here is [expressed by] '<s>yataḥ</s>.' '<s>Iyam</s>' — the meaning is: 'because it is not a [real] cause.' Then, what is the basis of the supposition? — to this he says '<s>api tu</s>' etc. <s>Vikalpāḥ</s> means 'positions' (<s>pakṣāḥ</s>) — conceptual constructs fabricated in opposition to the nature of <s>dhvani</s>, which is the soul of poetry, the substratum [established by] the semblances of valid means of knowledge and reasoning. Now, how can non-existence be constructed in the presence of [an] existent? — to this he says '<s>te ca</s>' etc. '<s>Tattva</s>' — the meaning is: 'due to the absence of the cognition of the true nature of <s>dhvani</s> as the soul of poetry.' '<s>Sphureyur api</s>' means 'they indeed appear.' '<s>Ata eva</s>' — the meaning is: 'since these positions are fabricated by delusion, therefore.' '<s>Atīta</s>' — [means those] whose ultimate purport (<s>paramārtha</s>) is past, i.e., refers to the past. There is also the reading '<s>paramārthatva</s>.' '<s>Paryavasyanti</s>' — just as in the root text, <s>jagaduḥ</s> employs the past tense (<s>liṭ</s>), so too in the commentary, the optative form '<s>ācakṣīran</s>' etc., though in the domain of supposition, also resolves into [the meaning of] the action's being superimposed by a cognition in the form of supposition — this is the meaning. He gives an illustration for what has been stated — '<s>yathā</s>' etc. '<s>Yadi nāma</s>' — this statement is for the purpose of generating dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) through revealing the truth of the matter. '<s>Kāyasya</s>' means 'of the body.' '<s>Yat</s>' — the meaning is: 'flesh etc.' '<s>Śunaḥ kākāṃś ca</s>' — it is implicitly understood that [they are] engaged in eating. '<s>Ityatra</s>' — the connection is: '<s>bhūtaprāṇataiva</s>' (it is only of the nature of past reality). '<s>Evam</s>' — the meaning is: 'by virtue of the internality of flesh etc. that has become external.' '<s>Locanam</s>' here [explains]: 'If the body were thus seen, then it would be perceived in this way' — this is only of the nature of past reality. 'If it were not so, then what would happen?' — here too: 'What has occurred? If, as before, there is no supposition of existence' — this is the very meaning. Enough of this digression from the main topic. Therein, according to those who rely on convention: considering that 'a word conveys meaning,' there is no <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning) beyond the expressed (<s>vācya</s>); or even if it exists, it is <s>bhākta</s> (figurative), being drawn out by the secondary function (<s>abhidhāvṛtti</s>), because it is attracted by the force of the meaning understood from the word; or even if it is not drawn out by that [secondary function], it cannot be articulated — like the pleasure of a husband in maidens who have not experienced it — thus there are exactly these three main types of disagreement. Among these, the denial-alternative has three varieties: since the beauty-causing factors of poetry are only the qualities (<s>guṇas</s>) and ornaments (<s>alaṅkāras</s>) of word and meaning — [being] made of beautiful words and meanings surpassing worldly and śāstric [usage] — the <s>Bālapriyā</s> [says]: '<s>kāyasya</s>' means 'of the body.' '<s>Evam</s>' — the meaning is: 'the world, in the sense of being like dogs and crows to be warded off.' By two sentences the essential meaning of the verse has been shown. '<s>Bhūtaprāṇataiva</s>' — the meaning is: 'it is only of the nature of a past state of affairs.' That is, the activity of becoming external etc., which is the domain of supposition, is understood as delimited by past time. To show that the same [principle applies] in the domain of prohibition as in [the domain of] injunction, he says '<s>yadi</s>' etc. This single-quarter sentence is the remainder of the verse '<s>yadi nāma</s>' etc. — '<s>yadi na syāt</s>' (if it were not so). The meaning is: 'if that which is inside the body were not to become external.' Rather, the body would remain with its inner and outer portions arranged just as they are — this is the purport. '<s>Tataḥ kiṃ syāt</s>' — the meaning is: 'what result would there be even then?' Even then, this body, being utterly disgusting, would be fruitless — useful only for the enjoyment of the most trivial objects — this is the purport. The connection of '<s>ityatrāpi</s>' is with '<s>ayam evārthaḥ</s>.' He explains the stated sentence — '<s>kiṃ vṛttam</s>' etc. The construction is: 'If there is no supposition of existence, what has occurred?' '<s>Tataḥ kiṃ syāt</s>' is explained by '<s>kiṃ vṛttam</s>' — 'Even then, what result has arisen? Nothing' — this is the meaning. The explanation of '<s>yadi na syāt</s>' is '<s>yadi na bhavanasya sambhāvanā</s>.' '<s>Pūrvavat</s>' is an illustration by contrast: 'just as in the case of "<s>yadi nāma</s>" etc., the supposition of existence [was shown].' '<s>Ayam evārthaḥ</s>' — the purport is: even in the domain of prohibition, the meaning of the optative (<s>liṅ</s>) is only supposition. Then, at the outset, to facilitate understanding, he shows the purport — by '<s>tatra</s>' etc. '<s>Tatra</s>' means 'in the domain of <s>dhvani</s>.' '<s>Samayāpekṣeṇa</s>' means 'with the assistance of convention.' '<s>Iti kṛtvā</s>' means 'for this reason' — i.e., because the word conveys only the conventionally designated meaning. '<s>Vācyavyatirikta</s>' means 'distinct from the conventionally designated meaning.' '<s>Vyaṅgya</s>' [means] 'that which is accepted as real [suggested meaning]' — 'does not exist in poetry' — the meaning is: what is accepted as <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested) is not communicated by poetry, because it is not conventionally designated by the word '<s>kāvya</s>.' '<s>Sadapi</s>' — the connection is: 'even if <s>vyaṅgya</s> distinct from the expressed exists, it is <s>bhākta</s> (figurative).' The reason here: '<s>abhidhāvṛttyākṣiptam</s>' — 'indicated by <s>abhidhāvṛtti</s>,' i.e., by a secondary function (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) that is the tail-end of denotation (<s>abhidhā</s>); '<s>ākṣiptam</s>' means 'made known.' The reason here: '<s>śabda</s>' etc. — '<s>bala</s>' means 'auxiliary.' '<s>Tadanākṣiptam</s>' means 'not indicated by the secondary function of denotation.' The carry-over of '<s>tatsadapi</s>' [gives] the construction '<s>sadapi</s>.' '<s>Vaktum</s>' means 'to convey by means of a distinctive property.' '<s>Na śakyam</s>' — 'there is no capacity' — the completion is: 'among the wise.' The illustration here: '<s>kumārīṣv iva</s>' — the locative expresses the intention of [being] the locus of the capacity of speech. '<s>Atadvitsu</s>' means 'among those who have not experienced the pleasure of a husband.' '<s>Pradhānavipratipatti</s>' — since these are stated in the <s>kārikā</s>, they have primacy. He states those very varieties — '<s>śabda</s>' etc. The <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) and <s>alaṅkāras</s> (ornaments) that belong to word and meaning — they alone [are the beauty-makers]. For these are the causes of beauty accepted by both parties. '<s>Śabda</s>' etc. — the meaning is: 'because they cause the beauty of poetry.' This reason should be understood [as applying] everywhere in what follows: wherever there is the causing of poetic beauty, there is the status of being one of word-quality, meaning-quality, etc. — the <s>Locana</s> [says]: 'There is no other cause of poetic beauty that has not been enumerated by us' — this is one variety. 'Or that which has not been enumerated [by us] is simply not a cause of beauty' — this is the second. 'Now, if it is a cause of beauty, then it is subsumed under the <s>guṇas</s> or <s>alaṅkāras</s> already stated by us — what scholarship is there in merely giving a different name?' 'But even if there is no subsumption under the stated <s>guṇas</s> or <s>alaṅkāras</s>, still, giving a different name by relying on some slight distinguishing feature [is no achievement], since the varieties of <s>upamā</s> (simile) and <s>vicchitti</s> (variation) are innumerable.' 'Even so, there is no actual distinction from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>.' 'And what is accomplished by just that much? — since other types of variety too can be imagined.' 'For the ancients like <s>Bharata</s>-muni accepted only <s>yamaka</s> (word-play) and <s>upamā</s> (simile) as word-ornaments and meaning-ornaments [respectively]; the elaboration and indication of their varieties was done by other <s>alaṅkāra</s>-writers.' 'Just as upon hearing the illustration "<s>kumbhakāra</s> (potter)" etc. in [the rule] "<s>karmaṇy aṇ</s>," one independently infers [forms like] "<s>nagarakāra</s>" etc. — what self-congratulation is there in that?' 'Even in this context' — the <s>Bālapriyā</s>: the universal rule (<s>vyāpti</s>) has been demonstrated by this. '<s>Loka</s>' — the words '<s>loka</s>' and '<s>śāstra</s>' refer respectively to worldly and Vedic language. '<s>Anya</s>' means 'other than <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>'; the connection is: 'there is none.' 'There is no cause of poetic beauty other than <s>guṇas</s> etc.' — this is the thesis; 'because there is no valid means of proof' — this reason should be understood here. 'Now, this thesis is not proper — because if such a beauty-cause distinct from <s>guṇas</s> etc. is established, denying it would be improper; and if it is not established, denial would be impossible' — to this he says: '<s>yo 'smābhir</s>' etc. The meaning 'accepted by you' is also implicitly established; and thus, the denial operates through the well-known counter-positive in the opponent's view — this is the purport. 'Now, since [in cases] where the form has been ascertained, denial is to be admitted only with respect to a particular property, by relying on the establishment of the nature of the qualified entity — denial of the very existence of the nature of <s>vyaṅgya</s> is not possible' — therefore he states the second variety: '<s>yo va</s>' etc. '<s>Na gaṇitaḥ</s>' — the meaning is implicitly: 'as distinct from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>.' '<s>Saḥ</s>' means: 'that which has not been enumerated by us but is accepted by you as <s>vyaṅgya</s>' — this is the meaning. 'Now, the beauty-causing nature of <s>vyaṅgya</s> is attested by one's own experience — how can it be denied?' — therefore he states another variety: '<s>atha</s>' etc. '<s>Saḥ</s>' carries over. '<s>Atha</s>' means 'if.' '<s>Antarbhavati</s>' — 'what is accepted as <s>vyaṅgya</s> must be one of the <s>guṇas</s> or <s>alaṅkāras</s>, since it causes poetic beauty' — this is the meaning. 'Now, through the name "<s>dhvani</s>" etc., the distinctness [of <s>vyaṅgya</s>] is established' — to this he says: '<s>nāmāntara</s>' etc. 'Now, it is not merely a different name, but there is also a reason for it — therefore there is no subsumption under <s>guṇas</s> etc.' — [the commentator] grants this objection: '<s>athāpi</s>' etc. '<s>Nāntarbhāvaḥ</s>' — the purport is: due to distinctive features like being the life-force of poetry. He refutes: '<s>tathāpi</s>' etc. '<s>Nāmāntarakaraṇam</s>' — the meaning is: you give a different name such as '<s>dhvani</s>' by relying on distinctive features like the life-force quality of our stated <s>guṇas</s> etc. He gives the reason: '<s>upamā</s>' etc. '<s>Vicchitti</s>' means 'variety.' '<s>Upamā</s>' etc. is a synecdoche (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) for other <s>alaṅkāras</s> and <s>guṇas</s>. He states the conclusion: '<s>tathāpi</s>' etc. '<s>Tathāpi</s>' means 'even so.' 'Then what [follows]?' — to this he says: '<s>tāvat</s>' etc. '<s>Tāvanmātreṇa</s>' means 'merely by giving a different name relying on some slight distinguishing feature.' '<s>Kiṃ kṛtam</s>' — the meaning is: 'no scholarship whatsoever has been achieved.' The reason here: '<s>anyasya</s>' etc. He substantiates that very [point]: '<s>cirantanaiḥ</s>' etc. He concludes the stated meaning with a sarcastic illustration: '<s>tat</s>' etc. '<s>Tat</s>' means 'therefore.' Or the reading is '<s>tatra</s>'; the meaning is: 'that being the case.' 'Therein, some might declare — word and meaning constitute the body of poetry. And among those, the causes of charm belonging to sound are <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) etc.' The <s>Locana</s>: this is the third variety. Thus one [basic position] has three sub-varieties; and the other two [positions make] five alternatives in total — this is the purport. He states those very [alternatives] in order — by '<s>śabdārthaśarīram</s>' etc. By the word '<s>tāvat</s>' (to begin with) he shows that no one disputes this [point]. Therein, word and meaning are not themselves <s>dhvani</s>, since what would be gained by a mere designation? Now, if the charm of word and meaning is <s>dhvani</s> — even so, charm is of two kinds: that which rests in the intrinsic nature alone, and that which depends on arrangement (<s>saṃghaṭanā</s>). Among these, the charm of words created by intrinsic nature alone [comes] from word-ornaments; that depending on arrangement [comes] from word-qualities. Similarly, the charm of meanings resting in intrinsic nature alone [comes] from <s>upamā</s> (simile) etc.; that culminating in arrangement [comes] from meaning-qualities — thus there is no <s>dhvani</s> distinct from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>. '<s>Saṃghaṭanādharmāḥ</s>' — the completion is: 'of word and meaning.' 'That which is distinct from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> does not cause charm — like invariable and variable defects such as <s>asādhu</s> (incorrect form), <s>duḥśrava</s> (cacophony), etc.' 'And <s>dhvani</s> is a cause of charm; therefore it is not distinct from them' — this is the negative inference (<s>vyatirekī hetu</s>). 'Now, <s>vṛttis</s> (styles) and <s>rītis</s> (manners) too are well known as distinct from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> and yet causes of charm.' 'And meaning-based [ornaments include] <s>upamā</s> etc.' 'And the properties of phonetic arrangement such as <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) etc. — these too are perceived.' 'Since <s>vṛttis</s> are not distinct from them' — the <s>Locana</s>: 'similarly, <s>dhvani</s> too will be both distinct [from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>] and a cause of charm — therefore the negative inference is invalid' — with this intention he says: '<s>tadanatiriktavṛttayaḥ</s>' etc. 'Indeed, the distinctness of <s>vṛttis</s> and <s>rītis</s> from them is not established.' 'For the three types of <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) have been called <s>vṛttis</s> for the purpose of distinguishing the three classes — roughness (<s>paruṣatva</s>), smoothness (<s>lalitatva</s>), and moderateness (<s>madhyamatva</s>) — by their utility for describing fierce (<s>dīpta</s>), soft (<s>masṛṇa</s>), and moderate [content] — because [they are] varieties of <s>anuprāsa</s> that operate within them (<s>vartante</s>).' As [<s>Bhāmaha</s> or <s>Daṇḍin</s>] has said: 'The arrangement of identical consonants in these three <s>vṛttis</s>...' The <s>Bālapriyā</s>: '<s>reka</s>' [means] 'distinction' — this is the meaning, according to some. The essential meaning of the <s>vṛtti</s>-text from '<s>śabdārthaśarīram</s>' up to '<s>pratīyante</s>' has been explained, and the following text is introduced showing its relevance to the main topic — '<s>nanu</s>' etc. '<s>Asiddho vyatirekaḥ</s>' — the invalidity of the negative inference [means]: the negative concomitance '<s>whatever is distinct from guṇas and alaṅkāras does not cause charm</s>' — [suffers from] deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) due to the <s>vṛttis</s> and <s>rītis</s> that are acknowledged as distinct from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> yet cause charm — this is the meaning. '<s>Ityabhiprāyeṇa</s>' — the meaning is: 'with the intention of [answering] this objection.' He clarifies that intention: '<s>naiva</s>' etc. '<s>Tahyatiriktatvam</s>' means 'distinctness from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>.' To show that <s>vṛttis</s> are subsumed under the <s>alaṅkāra</s> of <s>anuprāsa</s>, he says: '<s>tathā hy anuprāsānām eva</s>' etc. The connection of '<s>anuprāsānām eva</s>' is with '<s>vargatrayasampādanārtham</s>.' 'For what purpose is that?' — to this he says: '<s>paruṣatva</s>' etc. — the meaning is: for the purpose of distinctly presenting the natures of roughness etc. He states its purpose: '<s>dīpta</s>' etc. '<s>Dīpta</s>' means 'fierce,' in <s>raudra</s> (furious) and other <s>rasas</s>; '<s>masṛṇa</s>' means 'sweet,' in <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic) etc.; '<s>madhyama</s>' means 'moderate,' in <s>hāsya</s> (comic) etc. The 'describable' (<s>varṇanīya</s>) content such as <s>vibhāvas</s> etc. that is of such a nature — '<s>tadupayogitayā</s>' means 'by utility for the specific describable content, for the purpose of establishing the preferability of specific varieties of <s>anuprāsa</s>' — this is the meaning. '<s>Anuprāsajātayaḥ</s>' — the meaning is: 'types that are based on <s>anuprāsa</s>.' This will be elaborated further on. '<s>Vṛttaya ityuktāḥ</s>' means 'they have been designated as <s>vṛttis</s>.' He gives the etymology: '<s>vartante</s>' etc. '<s>Anuprāsabhedāḥ</s>' means 'varieties of <s>anuprāsa</s>.' '<s>Āsu</s>' means 'in them'; the purport is: in the word '<s>vṛtti</s>,' the suffix <s>ktin</s> is in the locative sense from the root <s>vṛt</s>.

children.translated_text: '— is poetry endowed with <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion)' — thus praising with affection, the dull one — we do not know what he says when asked by the wise one about the true nature of <s>dhvani</s>.

Thus. // 'Separately, separately' — [means:] <s>paruṣānuprāsa</s> (harsh alliteration) is <s>nāgarikā</s> (urbane [style]). <s>Masṛṇānuprāsa</s> (smooth alliteration) is <s>upanāgarikā</s> (semi-urbane), [also called] <s>lalitā</s> (graceful). [It is called <s>upanāgarikā</s>] because it is compared (<s>upamitā</s>) to the urbane (<s>nāgarikā</s>), i.e., the refined [style] — 'madhyamam' means 'neither soft nor harsh' — this is the meaning. For this very reason, the <s>vṛtti</s> (style) that is devoid of refinement, naturally neither delicate nor harsh, resembling an unsophisticated village woman — is called <s>grāmya</s> (rustic). Among those, the third is <s>komalānuprāsa</s> (soft alliteration) — thus the <s>vṛttis</s> (styles) are merely species of <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration). And here the <s>vṛtti</s> is not intended as in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> [system], whereby the <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments]: In the three <s>vṛttis</s> — <s>paruṣa</s> etc. — [the term] 'separately, separately' [means] the arrangement — i.e., the composition — of consonants that are uniform, i.e., of the same class — that is what they designate as <s>anuprāsa</s>. The three <s>kārikās</s> beginning with '<s>śa-ṣa</s>' etc. state the essential nature of the <s>vṛttis</s> such as <s>paruṣa</s> etc. — that should be examined in the original treatise. He glosses the portion 'separately, the <s>vṛtti</s>...' — '<s>paruṣa</s>' etc. The <s>vṛtti</s> in which there is <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) initiated by harsh consonants is [called] <s>paruṣa</s> (harsh). The very same <s>paruṣā</s> has the designation <s>nāgarikā</s>. '<s>Masṛṇa</s>' — the <s>vṛtti</s> in which there is <s>anuprāsa</s> initiated by sweet consonants is [<s>masṛṇa</s>]. He gives its two names — <s>upanāgarikā</s> and <s>lalitā</s>. '[Called] <s>upanāgarikā</s> because compared to the <s>nāgarikā</s>' — this is an etymologically transparent designation — thus he says '<s>nāgarikayā</s>' etc. The reading '<s>paruṣānuprāsaḥ</s>, <s>masṛṇānuprāsaḥ</s>' should be construed with the intention of [showing] the identity of <s>anuprāsa</s> and <s>vṛtti</s>. To show the middling nature of <s>anuprāsa</s> in the <s>grāmya vṛtti</s> (rustic style) to be discussed later, he explains the meaning of the word <s>madhyama</s> (middle) — 'madhyamam: neither soft nor harsh' — meaning 'different from sweet consonants and different from harsh consonants.' The <s>anuprāsa</s> initiated by those [middle consonants] is <s>madhyamānuprāsa</s> (middle alliteration) — this is the meaning. He states the designation <s>grāmya</s> for the <s>vṛtti</s> characterized by that <s>anuprāsa</s>, preceded by its derivation — 'for this very reason' etc. 'For this very reason' — i.e., precisely because of the absence of both sweetness and harshness. '<s>Vaidagdhya</s>' etc. — 'devoid of refinement' means naturally not delicate, not sweet, and not harsh, not having an intense nature; and a <s>grāmya vanitā</s> (village woman) [is of such nature] — from resemblance to her — this is the meaning. 'Among those, the third is <s>komalānuprāsa</s>' — among the <s>anuprāsas</s> mentioned, the <s>madhyamānuprāsa</s> is also designated <s>komalānuprāsa</s> — this is the meaning. By this, the established designation <s>komala</s> for the <s>grāmya vṛtti</s>, as stated by <s>Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa</s>, is shown. He concludes — '<s>vṛttayaḥ</s>' etc. Those [styles] which were propounded by certain [scholars] as <s>upanāgarikā</s> etc. — they too have come within the range of hearing. The <s>Locana</s> [comments]: In a class (<s>jāti</s>), the present existence of the individual (<s>jātimat</s>) would not obtain; rather, the present existence [of the individual] in that [class] is only through the class's conferral of properties. As someone has said: 'For kings exist in a transcendent dignity.' Therefore the <s>vṛttis</s> are not operations in excess of <s>anuprāsa</s> etc. — [they are] not operations that go beyond [those]. For this very reason, since there is no difference in operation, they are not entities whose essential nature is to be inferred separately — this is the purport [in saying that] the word <s>vṛtti</s> denotes operation. Precisely because they are not in excess, the designation <s>vṛtti</s> was not employed by <s>Bhāmaha</s> and others. Even though it was employed by <s>Udbhaṭa</s> and others, [the <s>Locana</s>] says 'they have come within the range of hearing' — with the intention that no additional meaning beyond [<s>anuprāsa</s>] has entered the heart [of the matter]. The <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments]: The <s>vṛttis</s> such as <s>paruṣā</s> etc., whose form consists of the arrangement of specific consonants beginning with <s>śa</s>-<s>ṣa</s> etc., in reality subsist in <s>anuprāsas</s>. Just as dignity [subsists] in a king — they are manifested by <s>anuprāsas</s> characterized by harshness etc. Just as the class <s>gotva</s> (cow-ness) etc. [is manifested] by cows etc. Therefore, because of the similarity of being expressible through their own substrates, the metaphorical application of the term <s>jāti</s> (class) to the <s>vṛttis</s> [is appropriate] — this is the import. 'But surely the statement that <s>anuprāsa</s>, which is the individual possessing the class, subsists in the class that is the <s>vṛtti</s>-form — this is improper, since it contradicts the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> doctrine' — to this he says 'na ca' etc. 'Here' — in our doctrine. 'As in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>' — as in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> doctrine. 'The <s>vṛtti</s> is not intended' — the subsistence of the <s>ādheyam</s> (that which is placed in a substrate) form is not intended — this is the meaning. 'Then what is the subsistence there called?' — to this he says 'that very conferral' etc. The conferral by the agent that is the <s>vṛtti</s>-form class — this is the meaning. And that [conferral] is the bestowing of differentiating properties by that agent, or the endowment with the capacity for <s>rasa</s>-suggestion. He gives an example for the stated meaning — '<s>lokottare</s>' etc. 'They exist in dignity' — meaning 'they are favored by dignity.' And the conferral by dignity as agent has the form of bestowing the capacity for accomplishing all tasks. In the <s>vṛtti</s> [text], regarding 'those whose <s>vṛttis</s> do not exceed that' — showing the referent of the word 'that,' he concludes — 'therefore, from <s>anuprāsa</s> etc.' He glosses [the compound meaning] 'those whose <s>vṛtti</s>, i.e., operation, does not exceed' as having this meaning — 'not in excess' etc. The operation of <s>anuprāsas</s> — which pertains to <s>rasa</s>-suggestion — that very [operation] belongs to the <s>vṛttis</s> as well — this is the import. Instead of saying 'not exceeding that,' he shows the result of expressing it thus — 'for this very reason' etc. The construction is: from the stated [fact], precisely because there is no difference in operation. 'Not entities whose essential nature is to be inferred separately' — without the apprehension of <s>anuprāsa</s> separately, they are not [entities] whose essential nature is to be inferred; rather, they are knowable through the inferential mark of <s>anuprāsa</s> in the form of the specific arrangement of consonants that manifest <s>vṛtti</s> — this is the import. There is also the reading 'not entities whose essential nature is to be separately denoted.' If there were an operation of <s>vṛttis</s> in excess of <s>anuprāsa</s>, then the essential nature of <s>vṛttis</s> would need to be separately denoted — that is the meaning [of the alternative reading]. He cites the approval of the elders for the stated meaning — 'not exceeding' etc. Regarding [the fact that] <s>anuprāsa</s> — not — by <s>Udbhaṭa</s> and others it was indeed done — to this he says '<s>Udbhaṭa</s> etc.' 'Employed' — done. 'In that' — in the designation <s>vṛtti</s>. 'No meaning' — the meaning [here is] the meaning of the word <s>vṛtti</s>. 'Additional' — additional beyond the meaning in the form of <s>anuprāsa</s>. And the <s>rītis</s> (styles) are <s>Vaidarbhī</s> and the rest. 'What then is this excess called <s>dhvani</s>?' The <s>Locana</s> [comments]: 'And the <s>rītis</s>' — the connection is: those <s>vṛttis</s> too, which do not exceed that, have come within the range of hearing. By the word 'that' here, the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) such as <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) etc. [are meant]; and in the bestowal of appropriate <s>vṛtti</s> upon them, [there is] a coming together in a composite form through mutual compatibility — like the flavors of jaggery, pepper, etc. in a beverage — [and this composite], whose domain is the <s>dīpta</s> (blazing), <s>lalita</s> (graceful), and <s>madhyama</s> (middle) [styles], [which arise from] the preponderance of usage in the <s>Gauḍīya</s>, <s>Vaidarbha</s>, and <s>Pāñcāla</s> regional [traditions] — that very threefold [composite] is called <s>rīti</s> (style). 'The class is not other than the individual possessing the class, and the aggregate [is not other than its parts]' — the <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments] with this intention. The passage beginning with 'they have come' is meant to convey the stated meaning — this is the meaning. Regarding 'and the <s>rītis</s>' — completing [the sentence] with the appropriate connected words, he says 'tat' etc. He states that the word 'tat' here refers to the <s>guṇas</s> — 'by the word tat' etc. The rest should be supplied. And such is also the reading. 'How indeed can the non-exceeding of <s>rītis</s> over <s>guṇas</s> [be established]?' — to establish this he says 'of those' etc. 'Of those' — of the <s>guṇas</s>. '<s>Samucita</s>' (appropriate) — the <s>vṛtti</s>, i.e., the special arrangement of consonants, that possesses the propriety of being suitable for the <s>dīpta</s> etc. [styles] — in its bestowal, i.e., in [the bestowal] of the <s>guṇas</s> upon that — this is the meaning. Some [say]: the <s>vṛtti</s>, i.e., the operation, that is appropriate for the suggestion of the respective <s>rasas</s> — in its bestowal, i.e., on the occasion [of such bestowal]. 'Mutual' — by the reason of mutual compatibility in conjunction — this is the meaning. The establishment of the threefold [classification] — '<s>dīpta</s>' etc. A <s>bahuvrīhi</s> [compound] with the word '<s>viṣaya</s>' [qualifying] a <s>karmadhāraya</s> containing a <s>dvandva</s>. '<s>Saṅghāta</s>' (aggregate) — the attainment of a different form through becoming a composite — that is [what is meant]. The example for the delightfulness due to composite form — 'like a beverage.' And thus the <s>guṇas</s> such as <s>mādhurya</s> etc. are not individually, in their separate particular forms, denoted by the word <s>rīti</s>; rather, [they are denoted] by virtue of possessing the distinguished property of the composite — this is the import. 'Now, by whom has this been stated?' — anticipating this doubt, he shows the basis for the application of the terms <s>Vaidarbhī</s> etc. and answers — '<s>Gauḍīya</s>' etc. The <s>Gauḍīya</s> etc. [styles] are [named after] the regions <s>Gauda</s>, <s>Vidarbha</s>, <s>Pāñcāla</s> — meaning 'of the poets of those regions.' The natural disposition or spontaneity (<s>hevāka</s>) in the domain of distinguished description — seeing that in preponderance — thus by him — meaning by <s>Vāmana</s> — this is the import. Or: by the perception (<s>dṛś</s>) of the preponderance of the natural disposition — by this reason — this is the meaning. Because it is observed in <s>Vidarbha</s> etc., it is named after those [regions] — this is the import. By [the word] 'threefold,' the threefold classification within <s>rīti</s> as <s>Gauḍīyā</s>, <s>Vaidarbhī</s>, and <s>Pāñcālī</s> is indicated. As <s>Vāmana</s> has stated: '<s>Rīti</s> (style) is the soul of <s>kāvya</s> (poetry). A distinguished arrangement of words is <s>rīti</s>. The distinguishing feature has the <s>guṇas</s> as its essence. It is threefold: <s>Vaidarbhī</s>, <s>Gauḍīyā</s>, and <s>Pāñcālī</s>. Because they are observed in <s>Vidarbha</s> etc., they are named after those [regions]. <s>Vaidarbhī</s> possesses all <s>guṇas</s>. <s>Gauḍīyā</s> possesses <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>kānti</s> (beauty). <s>Pāñcālī</s> is endowed with <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) and <s>saukumārya</s> (delicacy).' 'But by the stated method, since between <s>vṛtti</s> and <s>anuprāsa</s> there is a class-individual relation, and between <s>rīti</s> and <s>guṇa</s> there is a whole-part relation, how can there be identity?' — to this he says '<s>jāti</s>' etc. '<s>Samudāya</s>' means 'the whole'; '<s>samudāyin</s>' means 'the parts.' Others would say: <s>dhvani</s> simply does not exist. Since a type of poetry that differs from the well-established categories would lose its status as poetry — the <s>Locana</s> [comments]: 'the whole is not other [than its parts]' — [meaning] the <s>vṛttis</s> and <s>rītis</s> are not different from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> — thus that very distinguishing reason stands. Therefore he says: 'What then is this [thing called] <s>dhvani</s> that is different from those?' 'This [<s>dhvani</s>] is not the locus of beauty, since it does not have the nature of word-and-meaning. Nor is it a cause of beauty, since it is different from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>.' Therefore, even if poetry is relished through an undivided apprehension, if it is analytically divided through abstractive cognition, even so no additional meaning denoted by the word <s>dhvani</s> is obtained — thus he says with the word '<s>nāma</s>' (merely by name). 'But let it not have the nature of word-and-meaning, and let it not be a cause of their beauty — still, it would be different from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>' — anticipating [this objection], he states the second form of the <s>abhāvavāda</s> (denial doctrine) — 'others' etc. 'Let it be so; nevertheless, <s>dhvani</s> simply does not exist of the kind you wished to characterize. For it must be stated as something belonging to poetry.' The <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments]: 'Not other' — because the identity of those two is accepted — this is the import. He concludes the subject — 'thus' etc. 'It stands' — it is established. The passage beginning with 'what then is different from those' has the form of the conclusion of the stated inference — with this intention he introduces [it] — 'therefore he says' etc. 'Therefore he says' — therefore [<s>Ānandavardhana</s>] says. By the word 'tat' in 'what then is different from those' — which contains the reason within it — word-and-meaning and their <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> are referred to. In 'what is this' — the word 'kim' (what) intends to negate the alternative: 'Is this a locus of beauty, or is it a cause of beauty?' — with this intention he explicates — 'this is not' etc. A <s>dhvani</s> that is qualified by being a cause of poetic beauty and that is different from word-meaning-<s>guṇa</s>-<s>alaṅkāra</s> does not exist — and by this, the denial of the existence of <s>dhvani</s> so qualified is implicitly established — this should be understood. '<s>Eṣa</s>' — meaning 'that which is conceived as <s>dhvani</s>.' After 'thus,' 'the word kim' — the rest should be understood [as: 'is not said']. 'Since the meaning of the word "kim" is not obtained in the stated sense, [why use] the word "<s>nāma</s>"?' — to this he says 'therefore' etc. 'Through abstractive cognition' — meaning 'through analytical cognition.' 'He says with the word <s>nāma</s>' — the word <s>nāma</s> indicates utter non-existence — this is the import. By this much, the non-existence of <s>dhvani</s> qualified by being a cause of poetic beauty and different from word-meaning-<s>guṇa</s>-<s>alaṅkāra</s> is indeed established; but not the non-existence of <s>dhvani</s> in its own essential form — for establishing that, he introduces an alternative position — 'but' etc. '<s>Asau</s>' — that <s>dhvani</s>. 'Therefore' — meaning 'nevertheless.' Or: 'by the absence of being a cause of beauty' — this is the meaning. For indeed, because of being a cause of beauty, its inclusion within <s>guṇas</s> etc. was urged; if that [inclusion] is not accepted, then the existence of <s>dhvani</s> different from those remains worthy of consideration — this is the meaning. '<s>Guṇālaṅkāra</s>' is a synecdoche for word and meaning. 'Anticipating' — after the word 'thus,' 'initiated' should be supplied. The anticipation is: having taken to heart the objection of the <s>dhvani</s>-advocates — this is the meaning. '<s>Bhavatv evam</s>' — 'let it be so' — in the mode of concession. 'Then we have prevailed' — to this he says 'nevertheless' etc. 'But surely that existence [of <s>dhvani</s>] has already been stated' — to this he says 'of what kind' etc. 'Of that kind' — this connects with what precedes. 'Of the kind that was wished to be characterized' — meaning: wished to be treated as worthy of characterization by virtue of its connection with poetry. Showing this meaning, he says 'for of poetry' etc. The very nature of that which is aggregate — that it consists of word-and-meaning delighting the hearts of <s>sahṛdayas</s> (connoisseurs) — is itself the definition of poetry. And for a path that exceeds the established categories, that [definition] cannot obtain. Nor is it [something that falls] within that convention — the <s>Locana</s> [comments]: and that [<s>dhvani</s>] is something of poetry analogous to dance, song, instrumental music, etc. What is to be composed (<s>kavanīya</s>) is <s>kāvya</s> (poetry), and its nature is <s>kāvyatva</s> (poeticity). But dance, song, etc. are not said to be 'composable' (<s>kavanīya</s>). '<s>Prasiddha</s>' (well-known) — the well-known <s>prasthāna</s> (established category) is word-and-meaning together with their <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>; the path by which [scholars] traditionally engage in literary discourse — that is <s>prasthāna</s>. 'Of a type of poetry' — your intention is that this path is [a type] of poetry, since you have said '<s>dhvani</s> is the soul of poetry.' 'But why is that not poetry?' — to this he says '<s>sahṛdaya</s>' etc. 'Of the path' — meaning the endeavor of dance, song, eye-gestures, etc. 'That' — meaning the definition of poetry as 'that which delights the hearts of <s>sahṛdayas</s>' etc. 'But surely those who know such an unprecedented [thing] as a form of poetry — they alone are the <s>sahṛdayas</s>.' The <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments]: For [<s>dhvani</s>] must be stated as belonging to poetry by virtue of being a constituent [of it]. And when it is different from <s>guṇas</s> etc., its belonging to poetry cannot be established — like dance, song, etc. The formulation is: '<s>dhvani</s>, which is the subject of dispute, is not poetry, since it exceeds word-and-meaning; nor does it belong to poetry, since it exceeds <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> of those [word and meaning] — like dance, song, etc.' And the example is not deficient in the <s>sādhya</s> (property to be proved), since for those [dance etc.], the absence of poeticity and the absence of belonging to poetry are well-established because they are not 'composable' (<s>kavanīya</s>) — this is the meaning. The mention of dance, song, etc. as examples is made considering their special role of producing beauty in the domain of drama. With reference to his own stated meaning, he glosses the passage beginning with '<s>prasiddha</s>' — '<s>prasiddham</s>' etc. The gloss of '<s>pratiṣṭhante</s>' is '<s>paramparayā</s>' etc. '<s>Paramparayā</s>' — through unbroken tradition. '<s>Vyavaharanti</s>' — they conduct literary discourse. 'By the path' — by that which is equivalent to a path. '[But] the statement that <s>dhvani</s> is a type of poetry would be contradicted by the <s>dhvani</s>-denial doctrine' — anticipating [this objection], [the commentator responds] that the statement relies on the opponent's own position — he says '<s>kāvya</s>' etc. 'As a type of poetry' — as a variety of poetry. 'As such' — intended [by the opponent] — that is the meaning — this is the import. In the <s>vṛtti</s> [text], by '<s>prasiddhe</s>' etc., the previously stated reason is shown. 'Loss of poeticity' — by this, the <s>sādhya</s> (property to be proved) [is indicated] — this should be understood. '<s>Iti āha</s>' — 'thus, in response to the doubt, he says' — this is the meaning. He glosses the intended meaning of the word '<s>mārga</s>' (path) — '<s>nṛtta</s>' etc. By '<s>ākṣinikocanādi</s>' and the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.), other modifications arising from the eyes are included. The word '<s>prāya</s>' (approximately) is used as a synonym [for 'like']. '<s>Sahṛdaya</s> etc.' — meaning 'the definition of poetry as that which delights the hearts of <s>sahṛdayas</s>.' By '<s>sahṛdaya-hṛdayāhlādī</s>' (delighting the hearts of connoisseurs), the beauty consisting in <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> is stated. The <s>vṛtti</s> passage 'nor is it within that convention' etc. is a single [passage] comprising both objection and reply. There he explicates the objection portion — 'but surely' etc. '<s>Tādṛśam</s>' — meaning 'that which you [opponents] have contemptuously called comparable to dance, song, etc. — that essential nature of <s>dhvani</s>.' '<s>Apūrvam</s>' — unprecedented, not previously revealed. By [the word] '<s>jānanti</s>' (they know) — [the passage] 'certain <s>sahṛdayas</s> within that convention' — having posited certain <s>sahṛdayas</s>, even though the designation of poetry is applied to <s>dhvani</s> through their authority, it rests upon [its] universal acceptance by all scholars. The <s>Locana</s> [comments]: 'And that status of being accepted [by them] would itself become the definition of poetry only for that which exceeds the established categories' — anticipating [this objection], he says 'na ca' etc. Just as one who says 'I shall describe the defining characteristics of a sword' and then, describing [something] whose nature consists of extension and breadth, that can be worn as a covering, that covers the entire body, that is delicate, woven of variegated threads, capable of being folded and unfolded, that cannot cut, that is easily cut, and calling it 'an excellent sword' — when challenged by others saying 'What you describe is a piece of cloth, not a sword' — he would reply: 'This is precisely what I mean by sword' — with which every [opponent] is dismissed. The <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments]: The meaning of the <s>vṛtti</s> is explicated. '<s>Tatsamaya</s>' — the convention of the word <s>dhvani</s>. He glosses the portion 'for establishing that [convention]' etc. — 'that acceptance' etc. By the word <s>nāma</s>, he indicates that only the acceptance [by those few] would constitute the definition of poetry — [and so] 'anticipating [the objection], he says' etc. — meaning: having presented on one side the objection of the <s>dhvani</s>-advocates, he states the refutation. He clarifies the import of the refutation passage beginning with 'every' — with an example — 'just as' etc. 'The defining characteristics of a sword' — the essential nature of a sword. '<s>Karomi</s>' (I shall describe) — the root <s>kṛ</s> here denotes the action of speaking. Hence he will say '<s>bruvāṇaḥ</s>' (saying). '<s>Ātāna</s>' — <s>ātāna</s> means extension, breadth. '<s>Vitāna</s>' — lateral extension. 'Whose nature' consists of those. '<s>Pravriyamāṇaḥ</s>' — being made into a covering. There is also the reading '<s>prāvaraṇasvarūpa</s>' (having the nature of a covering). '<s>Saṃvartana</s>' — contraction. '<s>Vivartana</s>' — expansion. 'Capable of those' — suitable for those. '<s>Bruvāṇaḥ</s>' — meaning: calling the object qualified by extension etc. an excellent sword. '<s>Paryanuyujyamānaḥ</s>' — being challenged. 'How would he reply?' — to this he says '<s>īdṛśaḥ</s>' etc. 'An object of this kind is precisely what I mean by sword' — this is the meaning. '<s>Etat</s>' — meaning 'the definition of poetry stated by positing other <s>sahṛdayas</s>.' 'But what has been accomplished by this contemptuous statement? Nothing of ours has been cut [i.e., refuted]' — to this he says '<s>prasiddham</s>' etc. The object to be defined (<s>lakṣya</s>) must be established by the definition (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) — not invented [by it]. The object to be defined exists [independently] — this should be connected. 'Therefore he says' — meaning 'because of the stated reason, he says.' Meaning: he makes a statement in accordance with the stated intention. Since engagement is possible only in the domain appropriate to the minds of the learned, by the word '<s>vidvat</s>' (learned), the stated intention is indicated — this is the import. He states the result of the statement 'every [opponent]' — 'even the learned' etc. '<s>Tatsamayajñāḥ</s>' — those who know the convention of <s>dhvani</s>. 'But let there not be universal acceptance by all scholars; still, others might deny its existence or explain it otherwise' — [the third position holds:] 'there simply cannot exist anything unprecedented called <s>dhvani</s>. Since that [<s>dhvani</s>], which does not transcend charm (<s>kāmanīyaka</s>), is included within the stated causes of beauty.' The <s>Locana</s> [comments]: 'For even if this is done, nothing would have been accomplished — only madness would have been displayed' — this is the import. But one who explains the intention here [differently says]: '<s>Dhvani</s>, as a vital principle, is accepted by you; and what is called the vital principle is unprecedented, having not been stated by the <s>alaṅkāra</s>-theorists — and beyond the established categories — and that is not poetry: this is well-known.' All this [argument] of his is self-contradictory. For if he [the opponent] has accepted that [<s>dhvani</s>] as the animating principle of poetry, [and if] the prior dialecticians had not stated it — then this precisely makes it worthy of definition, not worthy of denial. Therefore, the earlier interpretation is [correct] here. 'But let it be a cause of beauty and included within <s>guṇas</s>, <s>alaṅkāras</s>, word and meaning — still, <s>dhvani</s>, by this designation, as a vital principle — this has not been stated by anyone' — anticipating [this] intention and presenting the third <s>abhāvavāda</s> (denial doctrine), [he says] 'but others' etc. '<s>Kāmanīyaka</s>' — the effect of the beautiful. Meaning: that which is the cause of the cognition of beauty. The <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments]: 'What is the fault [in this]?' — to this he says 'for if this is done' etc. [Meaning:] if a definition is constructed that consists of delighting the hearts of <s>sahṛdayas</s> — as newly devised — nothing of the nature of a definition would have been produced; rather, only madness would have been displayed, not learning — this is the meaning. He presents an alternative interpretation — 'but one who' etc. 'The intention' — the intention of the second <s>abhāvavādin</s>. '<s>Jīvita</s>' (vital principle) — the connection is: <s>dhvani</s> is accepted as the vital principle. 'And that' — meaning 'and the vital principle in the form of <s>dhvani</s>.' 'Not poetry' — the formulation is: <s>dhvani</s> as vital principle is not poetry, since it was not stated by the <s>alaṅkāra</s>-theorists. He refutes that — 'of his' etc. He demonstrates the self-contradiction — 'for if' etc. '<s>Tat</s>' — then. 'Not stated' — from the reason of not having been stated. 'Worthy of definition indeed' — meaning: it should be defined, not denied — this is the import. '<s>Prāktana</s>' — the earlier [interpretation]. '<s>Abhiprāya</s>' — the intention of the <s>abhāvavādin</s>. He introduces the third [form of denial] — 'but surely' etc. 'If so, what need is there for your effort?' — to this he says 'nevertheless' etc. 'Even so, that <s>dhvani</s>, by this designation, as a vital principle — has not been stated by anyone' — meaning: '<s>dhvani</s> is the soul of poetry' — this has not been said by any definer — this is the meaning. Therefore our effort is to state that, preceded by its definition — this is the import. 'The intention' — the intention of the <s>dhvani</s>-advocate. After 'anticipating,' 'initiated' should be supplied [as the remainder]. Since the root <s>vuñ</s> has the sense of effect, the statement of inclusion as a cause of beauty would be inapplicable — therefore he glosses — 'the effect of the beautiful.' He states the result — 'of beauty' etc. 'Of poetry' — this is understood. In the <s>vṛtti</s> [text], 'of his' — means 'of <s>dhvani</s>.' 'Among the causes of beauty' — means 'among <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>.' Of any one of those — merely making a novel designation — any kind of statement would result. Moreover, since the varieties of verbal expression are infinite, it may well be that in some minor aspect of poetry not shown by the established definers — [these people] dance [about crying] '<s>dhvani</s>, <s>dhvani</s>!' with eyes half-closed in the cultivation of feigned connoisseurship. The <s>Locana</s> [comments]: 'But since <s>vicchittis</s> (varieties of aesthetic charm) are innumerable, we have seen a certain <s>vicchitti</s> of such a kind that it would not be included in <s>anuprāsa</s> [and similar figures], nor in the defined <s>mādhurya</s> etc.' — anticipating [this objection] and offering a reply preceded by concession, [he says] 'since the varieties of verbal expression are infinite' etc. '<s>Vāk</s>' — that which speaks is <s>vāk</s>, i.e., word/language. '<s>Ucyate</s>' — that which is spoken is <s>vāk</s>, i.e., meaning. '<s>Ucyate anayā</s>' — that by which [something] is spoken is <s>vāk</s>, i.e., the function of denotation (<s>abhidhā</s>). Among these, the varieties of word-meaning diversity are infinite. The varieties of denotative diversity are also innumerable. 'A minor aspect' — for that [aspect] is a cause of beauty, [being] either a <s>guṇa</s> or an <s>alaṅkāra</s>. And it is already comprehended under the general definition. As they have said: 'The properties that produce poetic beauty are <s>guṇas</s>; those that cause its intensification are <s>alaṅkāras</s>.' Likewise: 'Indirect expression of word and meaning is considered the ornament (<s>alaṅkṛti</s>) of speech.' By the repetition '<s>dhvani, dhvani</s>' — indicating agitation through the repetitive expression — he shows [their] earnestness: 'they dance' etc. The definers of that [<s>dhvani</s>], the composers of poetry employing it, and those whose wonder arises from hearing such poetry — the <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments], having in mind the passage beginning with 'moreover, since the varieties of verbal expression are infinite' — which is about to be glossed — introduces [it] with the <s>Locana</s> — 'but surely' etc. '<s>Vicchittis</s>' — the various charms [so called because] they are variously 'cut,' i.e., differentiated — of those. By the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) after '<s>anuprāsa</s>,' <s>upamā</s> (simile) etc. are included. '<s>Uktalakṣaṇa</s>' (defined) — this qualifies both [<s>anuprāsa</s> and <s>mādhurya</s>]. Meaning: 'defined by you [opponents].' 'Preceded by concession' — by [the word] '<s>kvacit</s>' (in some case), the concession is shown. Regarding the word '<s>vāk</s>' in 'since the varieties of verbal expression [are infinite]' — [he explains] it as having multiple senses, and the word '<s>vikalpa</s>' as meaning 'variety' — 'that which speaks' etc. 'Diversity of denotation' — this, however, is stated in accordance with the doctrine of <s>Kuntaka</s> and others. He explicates the underlying meaning — 'for that' etc. 'That' — [refers to] the minor aspect. 'And that is a cause of beauty.' He cites the definition stated by <s>Vāmana</s> — 'of poetic beauty' etc. '<s>Tadatiśaya</s>' — meaning 'the intensification of poetic beauty.' He also cites [the definition] stated by <s>Bhāmaha</s> — 'likewise: indirect (<s>vakrā</s>)' — i.e., variegated, wonder-producing. 'Of the expressed and the word' — i.e., of meaning and denotative expression — the <s>ukti</s>, i.e., the <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation). And thus, whatever other variety of aesthetic charm is delineated, since it is comprehended under the general definition of the stated <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>, it is impossible that it should not have been seen by those [earlier authorities] — this is the import. 'By the repetition' — meaning 'by the doubling [of the word].' '<s>Saṃbhrama</s>' — meaning the haste of the <s>dhvani</s>-advocates in establishing the <s>dhvani</s> system. 'Indicating' — the doubling here indicates agitation — this is the import. 'Earnestness' — meaning the earnestness of the <s>dhvani</s>-advocates toward <s>dhvani</s>. Regarding the subject of 'they dance' — he supplies the appropriate agent — 'those' etc. The word 'tat' [refers to] <s>dhvani</s>. Some are definers of <s>dhvani</s>, some are composers of poetry employing it, some experience wonder from hearing such poetry — 'we do not know the reason for [their behavior].' For thousands of varieties of <s>alaṅkāra</s> have been elucidated by other great minds, and continue to be elucidated. And of those [earlier scholars], no such condition [of agitated dancing] is heard. Therefore <s>dhvani</s> is merely a rumor. No truth of it capable of withstanding scrutiny can be demonstrated. And thus, another has composed a verse on this matter: 'In which there is no real substance, not a thing that delights the mind, with all its ornaments' — the <s>Locana</s> [comments]: '[those addressed as] recipients' should be supplied. 'What is this excessive regard for the word <s>dhvani</s>?' — this is the import. 'This is the view. Self-conceit, and also being praised by others' — this is the meaning. Or '<s>vāgvikalpāḥ</s>' [means] the varieties of the creative activity of intuitive genius (<s>pratibhā</s>) that are the causes of verbal expression — thus also [it may be interpreted]. 'Therefore it is merely a rumor' — this is the common conclusion of all the <s>abhāvavādins</s> (deniers). Since [<s>dhvani</s>] is not different from <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> when it comes to being a cause of beauty; and since, when different, it is not a cause of beauty; and since, even if a cause of beauty, it is not worthy of special regard — therefore — this is the meaning. 'And this conjecture of non-existence is not without foundation' — [meaning] it has not been refuted — to this he says 'and thus, by another' etc. The <s>Bālapriyā</s> [comments]: By 'a contemporary of the author of the treatise' — 'recipients' — meaning by those three. Some, however, read: 'he shows disregard,' and 'not employing that in poetry,' and 'not [arising] from hearing that.' In that case, 'disregard' means the disregard of the <s>abhāvavādins</s> toward <s>dhvani</s>. 'Not employing that' etc. — since it is impossible to say 'the definers of that <s>dhvani</s>,' the expression resolves into referring merely to the word <s>dhvani</s>. And that becomes merely a cause of ridicule — this is the import. 'By others' — meaning 'by composers of poetry employing <s>dhvani</s>.' By the method of the lion's backward glance (<s>siṃhāvalokana-nyāya</s>), he glosses the word '<s>vāgvikalpa</s>' in 'since the varieties of verbal expression are infinite' differently — '<s>vāk</s>' etc. Since the <s>abhāvavāda</s> has been presented as mutually connected, [showing] the establishment of its unity, the conclusion too must be correspondingly [unified] — with this intention he says 'of all' etc. He makes explicit the commonality — 'since' etc. 'Not worthy of regard' — because, through inclusion within <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>, only the word [<s>dhvani</s>] is unprecedented — this is the import. The passage beginning with 'and thus' is intended to show the foundation of the previously displayed conjecture of the <s>abhāvavāda</s> — with this intention he introduces that passage — 'and this' etc. 'This conjecture of non-existence' — the previously displayed conjecture of the <s>abhāvavāda</s>. 'Not without foundation' — meaning not groundless, but rather well-founded — this is the import. [The reason for using] the past tense in 'has been refuted' — even though the refutation of the <s>abhāvavāda</s> is yet to come, because it is already mentally formulated and as good as accomplished — hence the past-tense usage. '<s>Iti āha</s>' — meaning 'with this intention, he says.'

children.translated_text: <s>Locana</s>: 'In the manuscripts' — with this intention, 'they call it figurative' is a statement with reference to the constantly-occurring present [tense].

children.text: bhajyate sevyate tadārthena prasiddhatayotprekṣyata iti bhaktirdharmo 'bhidheyena sāmīpyādiḥ, tata āgato bhākto lākṣaṇiko 'rthaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Bhakti</s> (devotion/division) — that which is served (<s>bhajyate</s>), i.e., is attended to by its [associated] meaning; or, that which is imagined (<s>utprekṣyate</s>) through its well-known [association] — that is <s>bhakti</s>, i.e., the property of proximity etc. to the denotatum; from that arises the figurative (<s>bhākta</s>), i.e., the secondary (<s>lākṣaṇika</s>) meaning.
As they declare: 'By proximity to the denotatum, by resemblance, by inherence,
by opposition, and by connection with action — <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) is considered to be fivefold.'

<s>Locana</s>: By a poet named <s>Manoratha</s>. Since it is not embellished (<s>salaṅkṛti</s>), therefore it does not delight the mind (<s>manaḥprahladi</s>). By this, the absence of figures of meaning (<s>arthalaṅkaras</s>) is stated. 'Composed by learned ones, and not at all, with words' — [this states the absence] of figures of sound (<s>śabdalaṅkaras</s>). <s>Vakrokti</s> means 'excellent composition,' and 'devoid of that' — [this states the absence] of the qualities of sound and sense (<s>śabdarthaguṇas</s>). Some [say] that by the word 'vakroktiśūnya' (devoid of oblique expression), the absence of all figures is stated through the absence of the general characteristic. By them, the [charge of] redundancy is not at all avoided — enough [of that]. 'Prītyā' ('with affection') — the meaning is: with a follower's blind attachment. 'Sumatinā' ('by the wise one') — [the idea is:] when questioned by the dull one, [the wise one] gives an answer only through frowning side-glances etc.; let him declare its true nature to his heart's content — this is the purport. Thus these conceptual alternatives of denial have come in a chain-like sequence, not disconnected from each other. For in the approach to examining the third type of denial, the very intention of the word 'punaḥ' ('again') is this, and the unity of the concluding summary accords [with this]. The reality of the denial-doctrine has been stated by way of its being merely a possibility, not a certainty. [<s>Bālapriyā</s>] indicates that the figurative doctrine is uninterrupted — '[the verse] beginning with yasmin.' 'Yasmin' means 'in which poetry.' 'Sālaṅkṛti' — therefore [it is] 'manaḥprahlādi' (mind-delighting). 'Kiñcana vastu' — 'some entity being described, some meaning, does not exist.' '[The verse beginning with] vyutpannaiḥ' — in the reading 'naiva,' 'yat' has a diminishing [force]. 'Yanna' is also a reading. 'Yat' means 'which poetry.' 'Vyutpannaiḥ' means 'rendered variegated through the employment of <s>anuprāsa</s> etc.'; 'vacanaiḥ' means 'by words.' 'Not at all composed,' and likewise that which 'is devoid of vakrokti' — such poetry, devoid of figures of meaning etc., 'is endowed with <s>dhvani</s>' — thus 'praising with affection, the dull one — what does he say about the true nature of <s>dhvani</s>, when asked by the wise one? We do not know' — this is the construction. [<s>Bālapriyā</s>] explains the purport — '[beginning with] yataḥ' etc. 'By this' — meaning 'by the first statement.' 'Is stated' — the remainder is 'in the poetry.' The connection of 'absence is stated' with 'of figures of sound,' 'of qualities of sound and sense' should also be understood. 'Saṅghaṭanā' — the remainder is 'of sound and sense.' [She] cites another interpretation — '[beginning with] vakrokti' etc. <s>Vakrokti</s> is 'beautiful expression' (<s>sundaratarokti</s>), and beauty is indeed variety (<s>vaicitrya</s>). That indeed is the general characteristic of figures — thus the meaning is that the absence of all figures is stated. [She] refutes — '[beginning with] taiḥ' etc. 'Gatā' — the going-after of what has gone is <s>gatānugatikā</s> (mere following). The suffix ka is derogatory. With the attachment of those [followers]. Or: gata means 'another's going,' anugata means 'following' — those who have this [characteristic] are gatānugatikāḥ. Without themselves examining, they merely follow what others have said — this is the meaning. With the plausible attachment of such [followers]. [She] explains the purpose of the word 'sumatinā' — '[beginning with] jaḍena' etc. 'Why' — to the doubt whether these alternatives have been explained as mutually connected — in conformity with the commentary-text, he says '[beginning with] evam' etc. 'Come in a chain-like sequence' — i.e., mutually connected. 'Whence?' — to this he says 'tathā hi' etc. 'The very intention of the word punaḥ' — in 'punarapare' ('again, others'), the word punaḥ. 'They call it figurative' — 'others call that <s>dhvani</s>-designated soul of poetry a quality-function (guṇavṛtti).'
Thus.

children.translated_text: <s>Bālapriyā</s>: 'Of the stated intention only' — this is the meaning. If however the word 'punaḥ' has a specializing force, then one should say 'apare punaḥ,' and setting that aside, the placement of the word 'punaḥ' at the beginning — showing the immediate succession of the subsequent [alternative] with respect to the previously stated type — conveys the connection: this is the purport. And the connection has already been shown by the introductory passage. [She] states another indicator — '[beginning with] upa' etc. The purport is: if they were unconnected, then there should be separate concluding summaries. 'Jagaduḥ' ('they said') — [she] explains its sense — '[beginning with] abhāva' etc. 'Is stated' — the remainder is: 'by [the word] jagaduḥ.' 'In the manuscripts' — in the <s>alaṅkāra</s> treatises. 'Nityā' — here the present tense (laṭ) is used in the sense of the constantly-occurring present, as in 'nitya (eternal): Īśvara (the Lord) exists.' 'Nityapravṛtta' is a rule of <s>Bhoja</s>. [She] explains the meaning of the word 'bhākta' (figurative) by giving the etymological derivation of the word 'bhakti' through the karma (object) derivation — '[beginning with] bhajyate' etc. To distinguish from [the root] bhañj (to break), she gives the meaning — 'sevyate' (is served). 'By what?' — to this she says 'padārthena' (by the word-meaning). By the meaning such as a bank (tīra) etc. that is signified by words such as Gaṅgā etc. — this is the meaning. 'But what is this serving by the word-meaning?' — to this she says 'utprekṣyate' (is imagined). The meaning is: 'is expected, i.e., is depended upon as the cause of its own cognition.' Here the reason — 'through its well-known [association]': meaning 'through the well-known instrumentality of proximity etc.' Or: 'padārthena sevyate' (is served by the word-meaning) is said figuratively. And by that, the speaker's or the listener's deliberation — which takes the form of imagining (utprekṣaṇa) the instrumentality of proximity etc. in the cognition of the bank etc. through the word Gaṅgā etc. — that is what is intended here, she says: 'prasiddhatayotprekṣyate' (is imagined through its well-known [association]). 'By the speaker or listener' — this is to be supplied. 'By proximity to the denotatum' — this is the connection with 'dharma' (property). 'From that arises' — i.e., cognized from the cause of proximity etc. 'What is that?' — to this she says 'lākṣaṇika' (secondary). The meaning is 'lakṣya' (that which is to be indicated). Here she cites the corroboration — '[beginning with] yadāhuḥ' etc. 'Its meaning will be explained by itself [later].' <s>Locana</s>: 'Guṇasamudāyavṛtti' — of a word whose function (vṛtti) is in a collection of qualities; the portion of meaning belonging to such a word that consists of sharpness etc. is bhakti; from that arises the secondary (gauṇa) meaning, [which is] figurative (bhākta). 'Bhakti is the intense faith (śraddhātiśaya) in the proximity, sharpness, etc. that is to be conveyed' — intending that the figurative meaning may also be obtained by the same method [as the secondary], she says this with the thought that it should also be stated through another approach — '[beginning with] guṇa' etc. 'Guṇasamudāyavṛtti' — that whose function is to convey the collection of qualities: this is the meaning. 'Of the word' — meaning 'of words such as siṃha (lion) etc.' For words such as siṃha etc., while denoting the universal siṃhatva (lion-hood) or the individual qualified by it, also convey — through implication — the qualities such as courage etc. that are inseparable from their meaning: this is the purport. 'The portion of meaning' — a part of the meaning that consists of the collection of qualities. 'Sharpness etc.' means 'courage etc.' In [expressions like] 'siṃho māṇavakaḥ' ('the boy is a lion'), only the partial quality of courage etc. is cognized: this is the purport. Some, however, explain 'guṇasamudāyavṛtteḥ' as: 'of that whose function is in the collective [i.e., the possessor of qualities such as] a boy etc., through the medium of the quality' — this is the meaning. 'From that' — meaning 'from sharpness etc.' — by the instrumentality of resemblance: this is the meaning. Then she also gives the meaning of the word 'bhakti' through the bhāva (state) derivation — '[beginning with] bhaktiḥ' etc. 'In that which is to be conveyed' — i.e., in that which is to be cognized. 'In proximity, sharpness, etc.' — now, in [expressions like] 'Gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ' ('the cowherds' village is on the Ganges'), the denotatum to be conveyed is the bank etc., not proximity itself. Likewise in 'siṃho māṇavakaḥ' etc., [the denotatum is] the boy's identity with a lion, or the excellence of prowess etc. This is clear in the <s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s> etc. And it will be stated later in the <s>Locana</s> as well. Therefore, how does the statement 'in proximity, sharpness, etc.' accord [with this]? To this, some [say]: this reading has come from scribal error; it should be read as 'pāvanatvādau' ('in purity etc.'). Others, however, [say]: since proximity etc. serve indirectly as instrumental causes, by the word 'sāmīpya' (proximity), purity etc. is intended through secondary signification, and by the word 'taikṣṇya' (sharpness), identity with a lion etc. is intended — hence there is no inconsistency. 'Śraddhātiśaya' — 'śraddhā' is the mental devotion (bhajana) of the speaker in the form of contemplation; 'atiśaya' (excellence) of that — this is the meaning. 'Tām' (that) — the meaning is: 'the purity etc. that is the object thereof.' Or: 'śraddhātiśaya' is the special cognition of the listener. 'Tām' — the meaning is: 'of the bhakti consisting of intense faith.' 'Āgata' means 'occasioned.' 'Lākṣaṇikaśca' — the remainder is 'word.' Though the etymological derivation is the same, she states a different meaning through a different base-form — 'mukhyasya ca' etc. 'Bhaṅgo bhaktiḥ' — the purport is: [derived from] the root bhañj (to break), with the suffix ktin. After 'iti' there is a continuation: 'from that arises the figurative.' 'Āgata' means 'cognized.' [She] states the result of the explained method of interpretation — '[beginning with] evam' etc. <s>Locana</s>: 'From that arises the figurative' — i.e., the secondary and the metaphorical. 'And of the primary meaning, the breaking is bhakti' — thus the suspension of the primary meaning, the ground [for suspension], and the purpose — these three being present, the basis for figurative usage is stated. 'The soul of poetry [is] a quality-function (guṇavṛtti)' — the purport of the co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is this: although in the variety of <s>dhvani</s> involving non-intended denotation (<s>avivakṣitavācya</s>), such as 'a mirror fogged as if by breath,' there is figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>), nevertheless that alone is not <s>dhvani</s> — since it [<s>dhvani</s>] exists even apart from that, in the varieties of intended-other denotation (vivakṣitānyaparavācya), and even in non-intended denotation itself, it is merely figurative usage, not <s>dhvani</s> — thus we shall explain. And so he will say —
'By figurativeness (<s>bhakti</s>), this <s>dhvani</s> bears a non-unity of forms from the variety [of its types];
And it is not so designated through over-extension or under-extension [of the term].'
