children.translated_text: <s>Locana</s>: Regarding novelty, this is the connection. First he cites an example of <s>atyantatiraskṛtavācya</s> (completely concealed expressed meaning) with 'a smile' and so forth. The terms 'innocent,' 'sweet,' 'splendor,' 'rippling,' 'tender-shoot-like,' and 'touching' are completely concealed expressed meanings. What is suggested through them—namely, the unaffected beauty, universal charm, inexhaustible reach, the power to soothe distress, the capacity to satisfy, the delicacy pervading all limbs, the continuity of that impression over all time, and the desirability of the union attained through effort—by these the well-known meaning of the smile and so forth is made a receptacle for different qualities beyond those ordained by the aged Creator <s>Brahmā</s>, and to that extent it becomes entirely unprecedented. This should be understood everywhere. 'Of this'—the connection at a distance is 'unprecedentedness alone shines forth.' Everywhere in this regard— <s>Bālapriyā</s>: 'A smile'—'a slight smile' means a gentle smile. 'Is innocent'—the remainder is 'this applies everywhere.' 'Tremulous and sweet' is a compound: tremulous and sweet. 'The splendor of a glance' means a glance endowed with splendor. '<s>Parispanda</s>' (movement) means extension. 'Rippling with waves of fresh <s>vilāsa</s>' means: replete with successive waves—that is, continuously arising sequences—of <s>vilāsas</s> (graceful displays) that are fresh, i.e., of-the-moment particularities. 'Fragrant with tender-shoot-like sportiveness'—having the fragrance of <s>līlā</s> (playfulness) associated with tender shoots; thus constituted. By the etymology 'that which causes delusion,' the word <s>mugdha</s> (innocent) in its primary sense indicates the capacity to cause enchantment, or alternatively the naïveté marked by the definition '<s>mugdhā</s> is one in the bloom of new youth' and so forth. Similarly, the primary meanings of words like <s>madhura</s> (sweet), <s>vibhāva</s> (splendor), etc. are sweetness of <s>rasa</s>, sovereignty, and so on. Since those primary meanings are obstructed here, the words <s>mugdha</s> etc. designate the smile and so forth through the figurative ground of resemblance to those qualities, and through that, special beauty and similar qualities of the smile and so forth are suggested—thus he says 'innocent' and so forth. '<s>Mugdha</s>, <s>madhura</s>' and so forth—the meaning is: the primary meanings are <s>mugdha</s>, <s>madhura</s>, etc. 'Completely concealed'—the implicit sense is: because of obstruction. The word 'by those' connects with 'what is suggested.' Here, according to the one-to-one correspondence: of the smile—unaffected, artless beauty; of the glance—universal charm and inexhaustible reach; of speech—the power to soothe distress and the capacity to satisfy; of the gait—delicacy manifested through tender feet causing slowness, and the continuity of playfulness at all times; of youth—the desirability of a union attained through effort. This is what is suggested. 'By those, a receptacle for different qualities'—this is the syntactic connection. The meaning is: becoming a receptacle for different qualities in the form of unaffected beauty and so forth. 'The aged Creator' is <s>Brahmā</s>. 'That'—the meaning is: the smile and so forth. The word '<s>iti</s>' has a causal sense. 'Everywhere' and so forth—the meaning is: thus it should be understood everywhere. 'Unprecedentedness alone shines forth'—in '<s>bhāvibhrama</s>' and so forth, of the smile and so forth,
of this verse: 'With the blossoming of charming smiles, with rolling eyes, with stumbling words,
with gaits languid at the hips—such <s>kāminīs</s> (beautiful women), to whom are they not dear?' //
Even though such verses as these exist, through resorting to <s>tiraskṛtavācya</s> (concealed expressed meaning) type of <s>dhvani</s>, unprecedentedness alone shines forth.

children.translated_text: The word '<s>iti</s>'—
the meaning is: thus it has been stated.
Through the mention of being restrained, what is implied is stated—'though forcefully proceeding.'

children.text: dhṛtaḥ vailakṣyādvimukhībhavediti punastasyāpyanārambhiṇaḥ sākāṅkṣapratipatti nāma hṛdayaṃ yātaṃ tu pāraṃ rateḥ // //
children.translated_text: 'Held back, lest in embarrassment he turn away'—and then, of him too who does not initiate, the expectant apprehension named 'the heart has crossed to the far shore of <s>rati</s> (love).' //

Even though such verses as these exist, novelty is achieved through resorting to <s>arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya</s> (expressed meaning transferred to another sense) type of <s>dhvani</s>. Novelty is likewise achieved for <s>vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> (intended meaning is other than the expressed) type also, through resorting to the aforementioned modes, as in: 'The bride, placing her face upon the face of her beloved who feigns sleep, stands still, her <s>cumbana-rasa</s> (delight of kissing) surging yet restrained by the fear of his awakening.' <s>Locana</s>: 'Novelty'—this is the connection. The second occurrence of the word '<s>prathama</s>' (first) refers to a different sense—it suggests its own meaning as transferred to a different suggested quality such as being unremovable, being preeminent, being extraordinary, and so forth. Similarly, the word '<s>siṃha</s>' (lion) too suggests its own meaning as transferred to different suggested qualities such as heroism, independence, and wondrousness. Having thus illustrated two sub-types of the first kind, he introduces an example of the second kind with 'the intended meaning being other than the expressed' and so forth. '<s>Nidrā-kaitavī</s>'—one who practices the deception of sleep, meaning one who pretends to sleep. 'Placing her face upon his face'—the point is: she is unable to relinquish even that much divine pleasure born of the touch of his face. Hence indeed 'of her beloved'—that is, because he causes such delight. '<s>Vadhū</s>' means a newly-wed bride. 'By the fear of awakening'—by the fear that her beloved might wake up—'restrained' means forcefully proceeding yet somehow held back. <s>Bālapriyā</s>: Even in the description of the four [smile, glance, speech, gait], in comparison with those, the description in 'a smile, slightly...' and so forth shines forth as entirely unprecedented—this is the meaning. And likewise in what follows. 'Un-'—the meaning is: the suggested quality that is in the form of being unremovable, preeminent, extraordinary, etc., is that different quality; 'in that' is the meaning. The meaning of 'heroism' etc. should be understood similarly. '<s>Kṛtaka</s>' (feigned)—the meaning is: deceptive. '<s>Tāvat</s>'—the meaning is: at first. '<s>Pārayati</s>' (is able)—the remainder is: the bride. The word '<s>iti</s>'—the remainder is: this is suggested. 'Hence indeed'—the meaning is: because of being the cause of such delight.

Or, for example— '<s>taraṅgabhrūbhaṅgā</s>' (she whose brow-play is like waves): <s>Locana</s>: the desire for a kiss was held back for only a moment by her. For this very reason, having made [her state] unsteady by repeatedly examining her sleep with full absorption (<s>ābhoga</s>), she remained so, yet she is not able to turn away from kissing entirely—this is the meaning. If such a one as she is kissed all over by me, she would become embarrassed and turn away—thus even that lover, who refrains from initiating the act of kissing all over, his heart experiences what is called longing-laden apprehension (<s>sākāṅkṣapratipatti</s>). The apprehension (<s>pratipatti</s>), that is, the state (<s>sthiti</s>), which is full of longing (<s>sābhilāṣā</s>)—such a heart is tormented by the budding desire (<s>ruharuhikā</s>), not fulfilled by the attainment of its fantasy; rather, it has reached the far shore of that supreme delight (<s>paranirvṛti</s>) whose nature is the mutual regard for each other's life as everything, yet which has not been fathomed by any experience whatsoever—thus <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic sentiment) is indeed brought to fullness. In the second verse, however, the kissing all over has been accomplished, and modesty (<s>lajjā</s>) is expressed by its own word. Even though <s>śṛṅgāra</s> is thereby nourished, still, compared to the first verse—because there is an impossibility of culmination through the successive series of restraints upon the flow of mutual desire— <s>Bālapriyā</s>: [the commentator] states, intending that the word <s>bhoga</s> (absorption) has the meaning of direct realization—'<s>ābhogena</s>' etc. '<s>nidrā</s>' (sleep): by the examination of sleep, that is, by the act of looking (<s>nirvarṇanā</s>) with the thought 'this one is sleeping'—this is the meaning. By this, the re-emergence of the desire for a kiss is understood. 'Having made [her] unsteady' (<s>vilolam kṛtvā</s>)—in such a way as to be accompanied by doubt about kissing. [The commentator] states the implied meaning—'<s>na tu</s>' (but not) etc. [The commentator] explains the second half—'<s>evam</s>' (thus) etc. '<s>vilakṣā</s>'—being embarrassed. '<s>iti</s>' is used in the sense of reason. '<s>api</s>' is used in the sense of addition with respect to the bride. '<s>ruharuhikākadarthitam</s>'—tormented by eager longing. [The commentator] states the implied meaning—'<s>na tu</s>' etc. After '<s>caritārtham</s>' (fulfilled), in some manuscripts there is the reading '<s>yadyapi</s>' (even though), but that is an explanation of the word '<s>nāma</s>'. '<s>kintu</s>' (rather) states the meaning of the particle '<s>tu</s>'. '<s>anubhavena</s>'—by the experience of kissing, embracing, and so forth—this is the meaning. '<s>alabdha</s>'—that in which immersion (<s>avagāhana</s>) has not been obtained—this is the meaning. Even though immersion has not been obtained, [the heart] has reached the far shore—there is an apparent contradiction at first glance. To show the novelty of this verse, [the commentator] says—'the second verse' etc. [He] raises an objection—'<s>tenāpi</s>' (even by that) etc. [He] resolves it—'<s>tathāpi</s>' (nevertheless) etc. '<s>paraspara</s>'—the successive series of restraints upon the flow of mutual desire, and its culmination—thus the verse beginning with '<s>ityādi</s>' has distinctness compared to the verse beginning with '<s>nānābhaṅgi</s>'.
The vast expanse of <s>rasa</s> and the rest is to be traced out by this method;

children.translated_text: <s>Locana</s>: <s>rati</s> (love) has been expressed, and since it describes the entry of both [lovers'] minds into a single state, it nourishes <s>rati</s> all the more. (2)

This path, characterized by <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, their semblances (<s>ābhāsa</s>), and their cessation (<s>praśamana</s>), is of vast extent, through the differentiation of <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) and <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents) in each respective case, as was stated earlier. All of this is to be traced out by this method. Because of [the support of] <s>rasa</s> and the rest, this path of poetry, having been trodden in many ways by ancient poets numbering in the thousands or even countless, attains infinity even among its own [subdivisions]. For each of the <s>rasas</s>, <s>bhāvas</s>, and the rest possesses limitlessness through its dependence on <s>vibhāvas</s>, <s>anubhāvas</s>, and <s>vyabhicārins</s> (transitory emotions). And with respect to each individual subdivision of these, the affairs of the world, when composed by good poets, are transformed into something different by the force of their will, even though they exist otherwise in reality. And this was demonstrated in the course of the discussion on <s>citra</s> (the pictorial/varied).

children.translated_text: And here a verse (<s>gāthā</s>) has been composed by the great poet—

children.text: atahaṭṭhie vi tahasaṇṭhie vva hiaammi jā ṇivesei /
children.translated_text: [Prākṛta:] Even things not so situated, she causes to settle in the heart as if they were so situated;
that speech (<s>vāṇī</s>), which is the domain of an extraordinary poet, triumphs over [all] particular meanings.

'The four primary divisions' (<s>maulaṃ bhedacatuṣṭayam</s>)—the two divisions of <s>avivakṣitavācya</s> (unintended literal meaning), namely <s>atyantatiraskṛtavācya</s> (completely concealed literal meaning) and <s>arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya</s> (literal meaning transferred to another sense), and the two divisions of <s>vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> (intended literal meaning with another as predominant), namely <s>asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning with imperceptible sequence) and <s>saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning with perceptible sequence)—thus these constitute the primary four divisions—this is the meaning. 'Having illustrated' (<s>udāhṛtya</s>)—by this, [the verse] '<s>taraṅga</s>' etc. is made clear as an example of <s>saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya</s>, being from the <s>Vikramorvaśīya</s>; the verse cited in the second <s>uddyota</s>, however, should be considered by the connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdayas</s>) as to how it serves as an example of that. The verse beginning '<s>nānābhaṅgi</s>' has not been found in its entirety. '<s>Alakṣya</s>'—means 'in the sub-divisions of <s>alakṣyakrama</s> (imperceptible sequence)'—this is the meaning. The explanation of '<s>anusartavya</s>' found in the <s>kārikā</s> is—'<s>udāhartavya</s>' (is to be illustrated). The explanation of the word '<s>prāk</s>' (earlier) in '<s>yathoktaṃ prāk</s>' (as stated earlier) is '<s>tasyāṅgānām</s>' etc. 'In the sense of <s>api</s>'—means 'in the sense of accumulation' (<s>samuccaya</s>)—this is the meaning. The connection is: 'this was demonstrated in that [verse].' [The commentator] supplies [the implicit word] regarding '<s>atathāsthitān</s>' (things not so situated)—'<s>bahir</s>' (externally). This means 'the world external to the heart'—this is the meaning.
[Sanskrit <s>chāyā</s>:] Even those [meanings] not so situated, she causes to settle in the heart as if they were so situated;
that speech (<s>vāṇī</s>), which is the domain of an extraordinary poet, triumphs over [all] particular meanings.

children.translated_text: By her grace alone, the subject matter that is the domain of the poet, being extraordinary (<s>vikaṭa</s>), becomes boundless. (3)

[Thus the <s>chāyā</s>.] In this way, the infinity of poetic meanings through their dependence on <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, and the rest has been well established. To demonstrate this very point, it is said— <s>Locana</s>: 'This was demonstrated' in the passage '<s>bhāvān acetanān api cetanavat cetanān acetanavat</s>' (even inanimate things as if animate, and animate things as if inanimate)—[in that context]. 'Even those not so situated externally, as if they were so situated'—by the word '<s>iva</s>' (as if), since there is no possibility of resting in either one alone, [the meaning is] that they are all the more of wondrous variety—this is the meaning. '<s>Hṛdaye</s>' (in the heart)—means 'in the most preeminent [place], which is the touchstone for all emotions (<s>bhāvas</s>)'—this is the meaning. '<s>Niveśayati</s>' (causes to settle)—whoever possesses a heart, in that person's [heart] she firmly establishes [those meanings] with immovability—this is the meaning. Therefore, they become particular meanings (<s>arthaviśeṣāḥ</s>) distinct from commonly known meanings. And they become so only when established in the heart, not otherwise—this is the meaning. 'She triumphs' (<s>sā jayati</s>)—she excels even over creators (<s>prajāpatis</s>) whose powers are limited.

Even things previously seen, in poetry, through the embrace of <s>rasa</s>,

children.text: sarve navā ivābhānti madhumāsa iva drumāḥ // 4 //
children.translated_text: all appear as if new, like trees in the month of <s>Madhu</s> (spring). (4)

For instance, there is novelty through the support of the variety of <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning) that has the form of reverberation (<s>anuraṇana</s>) arising from the power of words (<s>śabdaśakti</s>), within the category of <s>vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> (intended literal meaning with another as predominant) itself.
For example, of [the verse] '<s>dharaṇīdhāraṇāyā adhunā tvaṃ Śeṣaḥ</s>' (For bearing the earth, you are now <s>Śeṣa</s>) and the like—

children.text: śeṣo himagiristvaṃ ca mahānto guravaḥ sthirāḥ /
children.translated_text: '<s>Śeṣa</s> and the <s>Himagiri</s> (Himālaya) and you—[all] great, weighty, and steadfast;
since you whose bounds are never transgressed support the trembling earth'—

there is novelty through the support of the variety of <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning) that has the form of reverberation arising from the power of meaning (<s>arthaśakti</s>) in that same [category].
For example, of the verse '<s>evaṃvādini Devarṣau</s>' (When the divine sage spoke thus) and the like—
'When the talk of the bridegroom has been initiated, the maidens, with the rising of their <s>pulaka</s> (horripilation),
indicate their inner desire, their faces bowed down with modesty (<s>lajjā</s>)'—
even though such [verses] exist,
For example—
of [the verse] '<s>sajjei surahimāso</s>' (the month of spring prepares itself) and the like—
'When the pleasant season (<s>surabhisamaya</s>) arrives, suddenly there appear the delightful
yearnings (<s>utkalikāḥ</s>) of those who are passionate, together with the buds of the mango tree (<s>sahakārakalikāḥ</s>)'—

even though such [verses] exist, the <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning) that has the form of reverberation arising from the power of meaning, having its body fashioned by the masterful expression (<s>prauḍhokti</s>) of the poet, possesses novelty.

children.translated_text: For example—
of the <s>gāthā</s> (verse) beginning with '<s>vāṇiaa itthidantā</s>' (O <s>Vāṇijaka</s>, [behold] these elephant tusks), [consider] its meaning—
[Prākṛta:] 'The elephant cow's tusks, O my son, shed themselves each individually;

children.text: iasonhāeṃ taha kaho jaha kaṇḍakaraṇḍaaṃ vahai // //
children.translated_text: from affection [for them], tell me then how she bears the armlet of thorns.'

even though such [verses] exist, there is sheer unprecedented novelty. The <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning) having the form of reverberation arising from the power of meaning possesses novelty through having its body produced solely by the masterful expression of the speaker as fashioned by the poet. <s>Locana</s>: '<s>dṛṣṭapūrvāḥ</s>' (previously seen)—this should be taken in both senses: [things] previously [perceived] externally through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and other means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇas</s>), and [things previously described] by earlier poets. Poetry is analogous to the spring month (<s>madhumāsa</s>)— [the examples show] desire and modesty, and the yearnings of the passionate. What charm is there in meaning merely touched by words [alone]? And these examples have already been explained at length previously, so what need is there of repetition? Even though [a subject] has been touched upon by earlier poets, newness arises indeed through the grace of this particular method—this much alone is the purport of the text, and nothing more. <s>Bālapriyā</s>: [The commentator] states the meaning connected with 'trees' (<s>drumānvayin</s>)—'<s>bahir</s>' (externally) etc. [He] states the meaning connected with the [poetic] meanings—'by earlier [poets]' etc. '<s>kā hṛdyatā</s>' (what charm?)—and therefore from the verse '<s>kṛta</s>' etc., from [the verse] '<s>evaṃvādinī</s>' etc., from the verse '<s>surabhī</s>' etc., and from [the verse] '<s>sajjatī</s>' etc., there is novelty—this is the implication. '<s>Satyapi</s>' (even though) etc.—the remainder is 'of these.' The connection is: 'newness arises indeed through the grace of this method.'
'The slayer of the she-elephant's widowhood [i.e., causing widowhood to the she-elephant], my son, who fells with a single arrow —

children.text: hatasnuṣayā tathā kṛto yathā kāṇḍakaraṇḍakaṃ vahati //
children.translated_text: by the bereaved daughter-in-law he has been made such that he carries an arrow-casket.' //

evamādiṣvartheṣu satsvapyanālīḍhataiva /
yathā vyaṅgyabhedasamākṣayeṇa dhvaneḥ kāvyārthānāṃ navatvamutpadyate, tathā vyañjakabhedasamāśrayeṇāpi /
tattu granthavistarabhayānna likhyate svayameva sahṛdayairabhyūhyam /
atra ca punaḥpunaruktamapi sāratayedamucyate--
children.translated_text:
Thus is the <s>chāyā</s> (Sanskrit rendering). /
Even when such meanings are present, there is indeed non-absorption [in them by the reader]. /
Just as the novelty of poetic meanings arises through resorting to the varieties of the suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>), so too through resorting to the varieties of the suggestor (<s>vyañjaka</s>). /
But that is not written out of fear of the work becoming excessively long — it should be inferred by the connoisseurs themselves. /
And here, though stated again and again, this is stated as the essence —
Though in this relation of suggested and suggestor manifold [varieties] are possible,

children.text: rasādi-maya ekasmin kaviḥ syād avadhānavān // DhvK_4.5 //
children.translated_text: the poet should be attentive to the one [composed] of <s>rasa</s> etc. // <s>DhvK</s> 4.5 //
Though in this relation of suggested and suggestor manifold [varieties] are possible,
the poet should be attentive to the one [composed] of <s>rasa</s> etc. // 5 //

children.text:
asminnarthānantyahetau vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāve vicitraṃ śabdānāṃ sambhavatyapi kavirapūrvārthalābhārthī rasādimaya ekasmin vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāve yatnādavadadhīta /
rasabhāvatadābhāsarūpe hi vyaṅgye tadyvañjakeṣu ca yathānirdiṣṭeṣu varṇapadavākyaracanāprabandheṣvavahitamanasaḥ kaveḥ sarvamapūrve kāvyaṃ sampadyate /
tathā ca rāmāyaṇamahābhāratādiṣu saṅghāmādayaḥ punaḥpunarabhihitā api navanavāḥ prakāśante /
prabandhe cāṅgī rasa eka evopanibadhyamāno 'rthaviśeṣalābhaṃ chāyātiśayaṃ ca puṣṇāti /
children.translated_text: And in a literary composition (<s>prabandha</s>), the principal <s>rasa</s> (<s>aṅgī-rasa</s>), when woven in as one [unified whole], nourishes the acquisition of particular meaning and the surpassing lustre [of the work].

children.text: kasminniveti cet---yathā rāmāyaṇe yathā vā mahābhārate /
children.translated_text: If [asked] 'in what [example]?' — as in the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s>, or as in the <s>Mahābhārata</s>.

children.text: rāmāyeṇe hi karuṇo rasaḥ svayamādikavināsūtritaḥ 'śokaḥ ślokatvamāgataḥ' ityevaṃvādinā /
children.translated_text: For in the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s>, the <s>karuṇa-rasa</s> (pathetic sentiment) was threaded by the <s>Ādikavi</s> (first poet, <s>Vālmīki</s>) himself, as declared by his own statement: '<s>śokaḥ ślokatvam āgataḥ</s>' ('grief became verse').

children.text: nirvyūḍhaśca sa eva locanam kariṇīvaidhavyakaro mama putraḥ ekena kāṇḍena vinipātanasamarthaḥ hatasnuṣayā tathā kṛto yathā kāṇḍakaraṇakaṃ vahatītyuttāna evāyamarthaḥ, gāthārthasyānālīḍhataiveti sambandhaḥ // 4. //
children.translated_text: And that [<s>karuṇa-rasa</s>] was fully developed — [<s>Locana</s>:] 'The slayer of the she-elephant's widowhood' — my son — 'capable of felling with a single arrow'; 'by the bereaved daughter-in-law he has been made such that he carries an arrow-casket' — this meaning is quite plain; the connection is: even of the meaning of the <s>gāthā</s>, there is indeed non-absorption [i.e., the suggested meaning is not dwelt upon]. // 4. //

[<s>Vṛtti</s>:] In this relation of suggested and suggestor, which is the cause of the infinity of meanings — though manifold [varieties] are possible — the poet, seeking to obtain unprecedented meaning, should strive with effort in that one relation of suggested and suggestor which consists of <s>rasa</s> etc. /
For when the poet's mind is attentive to the suggested in the form of <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, and their semblances (<s>ābhāsa</s>), and to the suggestors as specified — the compositional structures (<s>racanā</s>) of phonemes, words, sentences, and literary compositions (<s>prabandha</s>) — all his poetry turns out to be unprecedented. /
And thus in the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s>, <s>Mahābhārata</s>, and such [works], the battles etc., though described again and again, shine forth as ever-new.
[<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] The meaning of 'of this type' is: of this variety of <s>dhvani</s>.

children.text: vṛttau 'śarīratvena navatva'mityubhayatra bhavatīti śeṣaḥ. 'ekakāṇḍavinipātī'ti chāyā, tasya vivaraṇam--ekena kāṇḍenetyādi /
children.translated_text: In the <s>vṛtti</s>, 'as the body, novelty' — the remainder is: occurs in both [suggested and suggestor]. The <s>chāyā</s> of '<s>ekakāṇḍavinipātī</s>' — its explanation is: 'with a single arrow' etc.
<s>Kāṇḍa</s> means arrow. // 4. //

children.text: mahābhārate 'pi śāstrarūpaṃ kāvyacchāyānvayini vṛṣṇipāṇḍavavirasāvasānavaimanasyadāyinīṃ samāptimupanibadhnatā mahāmuninā vairāgyajananatātparyaṃ prādhānyena svaprabandhasya darśayatā mokṣalakṣaṇaḥ puruṣārthaḥ śānto rasaśca mukhyatayāvivakṣāviṣayatvena sūcitaḥ /
children.translated_text: And in the <s>Mahābhārata</s> too — having a predominantly <s>śāstra</s> (doctrinal) character accompanied by the lustre of poetry — the great sage, fashioning an ending that produces despondency through the desolation at the conclusion of the <s>Vṛṣṇi</s> and <s>Pāṇḍava</s> [clans], thereby primarily demonstrating the purport of his own composition as the generation of dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) — indicated <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) as the chief <s>puruṣārtha</s> (goal of life) and <s>śānta-rasa</s> (the tranquil sentiment) as the primary intended domain.
And this has been explained at length by other commentators.

children.text: svayamevacaitadudgīrṇa tenodīrṇamahāmohamagnamujjihīrṣatā lokamativimalajñānālokadāyinā lokanāthena--- yathā yathā viparyeti lokatantramasāravat /
children.translated_text: And this was uttered by the Lord of the worlds himself — desiring to rescue the world drowning in the great delusion aroused by him, [and] bestowing the light of supremely pure knowledge — by [<s>Vyāsa</s>]: 'As the worldly fabric disintegrates as worthless,

children.text: tathā tathā virāgo 'tra jāyate nātra saṃśayaḥ //
children.translated_text: so does dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) arise here — there is no doubt about this.' //
[<s>Vṛtti</s>:] By him who composed his own literary work culminating in the utter separation from <s>Sītā</s> —

sutarāmeveti yaduktaṃ tatra hetumāha--prasiddhiśceti /
caśabdo yasmādarthe /

bālapriyā 'gītādipradeśāntareṣu' ityādikaṃ vivṛṇoti locane--bahūnāmityādi /

ayameveti /

asvaśabdābhidhāne abhimatasyārthasya svaśabdenānabhidhāne /

children.translated_text: Thus the meanings of the words '<s>Nārāyaṇa</s>' etc. are <s>Viṣṇu</s> etc., and their intended designation [is established]. Therefore it is established: when poetry is composed with the principal <s>rasa</s> etc. as the basis, there is the acquisition of new meanings, and a great luster of style (<s>bandhacchāyā</s>) is achieved.

children.text: ata eva ca rasānuguṇārthaviśeṣopanibandhamalaṅkārāntaravirahe 'pi chāyātiśayayogi lakṣye dṛśyate /
children.translated_text: And for this very reason, even in the absence of other figures of speech, when meaning-details (<s>arthaviśeṣa</s>) are composed in accordance with the [principal] <s>rasa</s>, a surplus of stylistic luster is observed in exemplary [poetry].
For example — 'Victorious is the sage, the lord of <s>yogīs</s>, the great soul born from the pot (<s>Kumbhasaṃbhava</s>, i.e., <s>Agastya</s>),
by whom in a single small well (<s>ekaculaka</s>) those two divine [creatures] were seen — the fish and the tortoise.' //

[<s>Locana</s>:] By the word '<s>atyanta</s>' (absolute/complete), through the sense of being unconditional, he dispels the apprehension of love-in-separation (<s>vipralambha</s>). /
The mutual destruction of the <s>Vṛṣṇis</s>, the affliction of the <s>Pāṇḍavas</s> too — an inappropriate calamity through the hardships of the great path — and the destruction of <s>Kṛṣṇa</s> too by a hunter — thus, the conclusion of everything is disenchanting (<s>virasa</s>) alone. /
'Primarily' (<s>mukhyatayā</s>) — /
although it was stated '<s>dharme cārthe ca kāme ca mokṣe ca</s>' (in <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, <s>kāma</s>, and <s>mokṣa</s>), nevertheless the four '<s>ca</s>'-particles convey this: although the totality of <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, and <s>kāma</s> — such that what is not found elsewhere does not exist [there] — is of that nature, still, let the disenchanting conclusion be observed in these very [three aims]. /
But regarding <s>mokṣa</s> — whatever form it has — let its supreme value be contemplated here alone. /
'In proportion as' (<s>yathāyatha</s>) — /
what is esteemed as real (<s>vastubhūtatayā</s>) by people striving [for it] — what is assiduously pursued — of the nature of <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, <s>kāma</s>, and the means to their attainment — /
by whatever mode of acquisition, preservation, loss, etc. — /
[it turns out to be] insubstantial, trivial like an illusion (<s>indrajāla</s>), like <s>Indra</s>'s rainbows — /
'turns into the opposite' (<s>viparyeti</s>) — /
rather, the opposite comes about. /
The meaning is: leave aside the contemplation of its true nature. /
By that mode, in this worldly enterprise (<s>lokatantra</s>). /
'Dispassion arises' — by this, the <s>nirveda</s> (world-weariness) arising from the knowledge of truth — [<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] regarding 'up to the absolute separation from <s>Sītā</s>' — she states the purpose of the word '<s>atyanta</s>' (absolute) — 'by the word <s>atyanta</s>' etc. /
She elaborates the stated 'disenchanting conclusion of the <s>Vṛṣṇis</s> and <s>Pāṇḍavas</s>' — 'of the <s>Vṛṣṇis</s>' etc. /
Anticipating the objection that the statement '<s>mokṣa</s> as the <s>puruṣārtha</s> (supreme aim of life) is primarily the intended meaning' is unjustified, she resolves it — with 'although' etc. /
'And in <s>mokṣa</s> — it was stated' — /
in some texts there is also the reading '<s>bharatarṣabha yadihāsti tadanyatra yannehāsti na tat kvacit</s>' (O best of <s>Bharatas</s>, what is here is elsewhere; what is not here is nowhere). /
'Thus they convey' — /
the meaning is: they indicate the distinction to be stated. /
'The totality' — /
the meaning is: the principal, essential nature. /
'Does not exist' — /
'here' is the remainder. /
The syntactic connection is: what does not exist elsewhere — such [a thing] does not exist here. /
The purport is: what exists here also exists elsewhere. /
She shows the distinction to be indicated — 'nevertheless' etc. /
'Disenchanting conclusion' — /
'of <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, and <s>kāma</s>' is carried over. /
She explains 'worldly enterprise' (<s>lokatantra</s>) — 'by people' etc. /
'Etc.' — he recounts at great length. /
And thus the <s>śānta rasa</s> (tranquil sentiment) — by other <s>rasas</s>, and the supreme aim (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) characterized by <s>mokṣa</s> — by other <s>puruṣārthas</s> — being accompanied as subordinate [elements], is the intended principal meaning [of the <s>Mahābhārata</s>] — the purport of the <s>Mahābhārata</s> shines forth with perfect clarity. /
And the subordinate-principal relationship of the <s>rasas</s>, just like that [of <s>rasas</s>], has already been demonstrated. /
The charm [arising] through the self-sufficiency of the subordinate <s>rasa</s> — which is like a limb of the body — and of the <s>puruṣārtha</s> — is also not contradicted. /
Objection: however much is the intended meaning of the <s>Mahābhārata</s>, all of it is enumerated in the <s>Anukramaṇī</s> (introductory index); but this [<s>śānta</s> as principal] is not seen there. Rather, the status of the <s>Mahābhārata</s> as a cause of awakening to all <s>puruṣārthas</s> and as containing all <s>rasas</s> — is apprehended in that section as declared in its own words. /
To this it is replied: True — the principality of <s>śānta rasa</s> in the <s>Mahābhārata</s> and the supremacy of <s>mokṣa</s> over all <s>puruṣārthas</s> — this was not shown in the <s>Anukramaṇī</s> as something expressed in its own words (<s>svaśabdābhidheyatvena</s>); but it was shown as something suggested (<s>vyaṅgyatvena</s>) — in this sentence: '<s>Bhagavān Vāsudeva</s>, the eternal one, is celebrated herein.' /
For by this, the following meaning was intended suggestively: whatever in this <s>Mahābhārata</s> — the narratives of the <s>Pāṇḍavas</s> etc. — is celebrated, all of that is disenchanting in its conclusion, of the nature of the proliferation of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>); but the Blessed <s>Vāsudeva</s>, who is the reality of the supreme truth (<s>paramārthasatya</s>), is celebrated herein. /
Therefore, let your minds be devoted to that very Supreme Lord, the Blessed One; do not be attached to the insubstantial glories, nor be entirely absorbed in mere qualities like conduct, discipline, valor, etc. /
And further ahead — 'Behold the insubstantiality of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence)' — [<s>Locana</s>:] by one who suggests this very meaning, the <s>sthāyin</s> (permanent emotion) of <s>śānta rasa</s> is indicated; and through the demonstration of the insubstantiality of everything else, its principality is stated. /
Objection: but the aesthetic rapture of <s>śṛṅgāra</s>, <s>vīra</s>, etc. also shines forth there — anticipating this, he says: 'from the ultimate standpoint' etc. /
For people engrossed in sensual enjoyment, possessed by worldly <s>vāsanā</s> (habitual impressions), even toward a subordinate <s>rasa</s>, there is such a sense of [its] importance, just as toward the body there is the self-conception of being a knower (<s>pramātṛtvābhimāna</s>) even though it is merely the locus of experience; 'mere' — serving as instruments of devotion to the Supreme Lord — [<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] 'as real' — /
the meaning is: in the ultimate sense. /
'Trivial' — /
trivial like a hare's horn etc. /
'Of that very' — /
the meaning is: of <s>śānta rasa</s> alone. /
She introduces the passage 'from the ultimate standpoint' etc. — 'objection' etc. /
'There' — in the <s>Mahābhārata</s>. /
She elaborates the purport — 'for those engrossed in enjoyment' etc. /
'Such a sense of importance' — the sense of principality. /
'Toward the body, merely' — this is the syntactic connection. /
'Illuminating' — the word (<s>śabda</s>) shines forth — this is the connection. /
'Entirely' (<s>nyakṣeṇa</s>) — /
the meaning is: completely. /
The construal is: the description as a means to attainment. /
Regarding 'of [the specific] deities' — 'description of the special powers' is carried over. /
'Of <s>mokṣa</s>' — /
the meaning is: of the cessation of ignorance. /
The construal is: <s>Brahman</s> is intended as denoted by the name '<s>Vāsudeva</s>.' /
'By that designation' — by being denoted by the name '<s>Vāsudeva</s>.' /
The <s>Māthura</s> (i.e., at <s>Mathurā</s>) manifestation — by which [manifestation] the complete essential nature was replicated. /
'Not merely' etc. — /
'Intended' — is carried over by transposition. /
She states another reason as well — 'in the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s> etc.' etc. /
'<s>Puruṣārtha</s>' — the connection of this is with 'intended.' /
And in the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s> etc., because the usage of the Lord under another name — under another divine form — is observed. /
And this meaning has been determined by those who know the truth of words (<s>śabdatattvavid</s>) themselves. /
Thus, by the sentence indicated in the <s>Anukramaṇī</s>, through one that illuminates the impermanence of everything other than the Blessed Lord, the supreme aim characterized by <s>mokṣa</s> alone [is shown to be the principal] — in the doctrinal view (<s>śāstranaya</s>); and in the poetic view (<s>kāvyanaya</s>), the <s>śānta rasa</s>, characterized by the nourishment of the happiness that comes from the extinction of craving — is the intended principal meaning of the <s>Mahābhārata</s>: this has been well demonstrated. /
And because this meaning is of the supremely essential nature, it was shown as suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>) only, not as expressed (<s>vācya</s>). /
For an essential meaning, when illuminated by not being directly named in its own words, brings forth beauty all the more. /
And this convention indeed exists among learned and refined assemblies: that the most cherished thing is revealed suggestively, not through direct verbal expression. /
[<s>Locana</s>:] The purport determined in the opening [verse] etc. is: this form-aspect is what is denoted by that name [<s>Vāsudeva</s>]. /
'And it has been determined' — /
for words, being eternal, were subsequently designated [to their referents] by the force of coincidence (<s>kākatālīya</s>) — as was stated in the <s>Kāśikāvṛtti</s> on '<s>ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaśca</s>' etc. /
'In the doctrinal view' — /
therein, in the absence of aesthetic relishing, [the aim] is sought by a person as useful — this designation alone is respectful (<s>sādara</s>); but when there is the conjunction of aesthetic rapture, the designation '<s>rasa</s>' [is used] — this is the purport. /
And this was stated by the author at length in the <s>Tattvāloka</s>; but since this is not its primary occasion here, we have not presented that. /
Regarding the statement 'all the more so' — she states the reason: 'and the convention' etc. /
The word '<s>ca</s>' (and) is in the sense of 'because.' /
Since this worldly convention is beginningless, therefore even for the Blessed <s>Vyāsa</s> and others, this very [convention] was the reason for not naming [the essential meaning] in its own words; otherwise, in the ascertainment of the action-agent relationship etc., and in the determination of the meaning of words such as '<s>nārāyaṇaṃ namaskṛtya</s>' (having saluted <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>), [we would ask:] what is the authority for [the claim that] such was the intention of the Blessed One? — this is the purport. /
By the mention of 'learned and refined,' the doctrinal view and the poetic view are both followed. /
What was stated — 'in this, the poet should be attentive, [for poetry] is made of <s>rasas</s> etc.' — that very [point], after the incidentally arisen determination of the connection with the <s>Mahābhārata</s>, he now concludes — 'therefore it is established' etc. /
[<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] She elaborates 'in the <s>Gītā</s> and other passages' etc. stated in the <s>Locana</s> — 'of many births' etc. /
'By the force of coincidence' — the meaning is: by chance. /
The syntactic connection is: 'was stated here' [in that context]. /
'In the <s>Kāśikāvṛtti</s>' is the remainder. /
She elaborates what was stated — 'in the doctrinal view, <s>mokṣa</s> is the <s>puruṣārtha</s>; in the poetic view, <s>śānta rasa</s>' — with 'therein' etc. /
'Respectful' — /
the meaning is: worthy. /
'In the sense of because' — /
the meaning is: in the causal sense. /
'This very' — /
the meaning is: the stated convention among learned and refined assemblies. /
'For not naming in its own words' — for not denoting the cherished meaning in its own words. /
'The reason' — the cherished cause. /
Here she states the corroboration — 'otherwise' etc. /
In the verses '<s>nārāyaṇaṃ namaskṛtya</s>' etc., the connection of the meaning of '<s>Nārāyaṇa</s>' etc. with salutation etc. through the relation of action and agent etc. is the intended [meaning]. /
Similarly, the connection of the meaning of '<s>Nārāyaṇa</s>' etc. with salutation etc. through the relation of action and agent etc. is the intended [meaning]. /

children.translated_text: [Vṛtti:] What is well-known to the world, even if marvelous, does not produce a sense of wonder.
Nor is the novel content, when employed, congruent only with the <s>adbhuta rasa</s> but also with other <s>rasas</s>.
[Vṛtti:] For example — 'She perspires, she gets goose-bumps, she trembles — the one attached to the tip of the street-balance;

children.text: sopāso ajja vi suhaa jeṇāsi volīṇo // //
children.translated_text: that side of yours, O fortunate one, by which you passed beyond [her], even today perspires.' //

[Locana:] In this and similar cases, the seeing of the fish and the tortoise in a single small well — being congruent with the <s>adbhuta</s> (marvelous) <s>rasa</s> — nourishes the poetic luster (<s>chāyātiśaya</s>). For indeed, in that single small well, the seeing of the divine fish and tortoise — even despite the proximity of the entire ocean — is more congruent with the <s>adbhuta rasa</s> because of its novelty (<s>akṣuṇṇatva</s>). For what is hackneyed is [merely] what catches the eye — and from that... Since this is so established, what is also seen in the illustrative [verse] is well-grounded; otherwise it would be unjustified — and yet it is not unjustified, because of the perception of beauty. The cause of that [beauty] is nothing other than the meaning being congruent with <s>rasa</s> — this is the intended purport. 'Of another ornament' — the word 'other' (<s>antara</s>) denotes 'specific.' Or alternatively, since in the cited example the ornament <s>rasavat</s> (rasa-possessing) is present, in relation to that, the word 'another ornament' [is used]. [Objection:] Surely, what is understood from the seeing of the fish and tortoise — namely, the proximity of the ocean to that single small well — and from that, the apprehension of the sage's greatness — so it is not the <s>rasa</s>-congruent meaning that nourishes the luster. Anticipating this, he says 'for here' etc. [Further objection:] Even so, let the inferred sight of the ocean be itself congruent with the <s>adbhuta</s> — then in this respect, how is this an example of a <s>rasa</s>-congruent expressed meaning? Anticipating this, he says 'for there' etc. 'For what is hackneyed' — that which, through repeated description and examination, has become trite and whose form is all too clearly known — this is the meaning. And this [principle] encompasses many illustrative cases — the <s>Bālapriyā</s> follows popular convention — this is the purport. He explicates from 'therefore' up to 'is seen [in the illustration]' — with 'since' etc. 'Of that' means: because of the perception of beauty — this is the meaning. He explains the word 'another ornament' in the [phrase] 'even in the absence of another ornament' in two ways — with 'the word "another ornament"' etc. '<s>Iti</s>' is [used] in the sense of 'because.' 'Not' etc. — Rather, it is by the stated <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning) alone that the luster is nourished — this is the purport. In the <s>Vṛtti</s>: 'congruent with the <s>adbhuta rasa</s>' — means: congruent with the <s>adbhuta rasa</s> supported by the sage. 'By coincidence (<s>kākatālīya</s>)' — this is an explanation of the implied meaning. '<s>Pratilagna</s>' (attached) — means: connected with the hero's side. '<s>Asi</s>' is an indeclinable in the sense of 'you.' 'O fortunate one, you — by whatever side of hers you passed — that side of the street where the balance-tip rested, that side of hers perspires even today' — thus the syntactic connection. 'Mutually' — from the passing by in side-contact, the love belonging to the hero too is apprehended — this is the purport.

rasapratītiriti /

children.translated_text: [Locana:] Among all the varieties of <s>dhvani</s>, their subordination [to the expressed] produces infinitude — thus he says: 'too prolix' etc.
'By themselves' etc.

children.text: tatra vastunā vyaṅgyena guṇībhūtena navatvaṃ satyapa purāṇārthasparśe yathā mamaiva-- bhaavihalarakhkhaṇekakamallasaraṇāgaāṇaaththāṇa /
children.translated_text: [Vṛtti:] Therein, novelty arising from subordinated suggested content (<s>vastu vyaṅgya</s>), even when the expressed meaning has been touched by earlier poets — for example, by myself: 'Of wealth — for those who are shelterless, who have taken refuge in the single champion, exhausted from the wandering through the chain of protectors overcome by fear —
not even a moment's respite (<s>viśrāmakathā</s>) has been granted — this is fitting indeed!' //

[Locana:] Whatever <s>rasa</s>-apprehension arises from the content being evoked in this <s>gāthā</s> (Prakrit verse) — that [apprehension] does not arise even slightly from such content as 'having touched you, she perspires, she gets goose-bumps, she trembles.' Thus, through the classification of <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion), it has been demonstrated how novelty (<s>navatva</s>) arises in poetic content. Even through the classification of <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> (suggestion subordinated to the expressed), in its three varieties with respect to what is suggested — novelty of poetic content arises in just the same way. But since [elaborating on] that would be too prolix, it has not been illustrated — the connoisseurs should deduce it themselves. The <s>Locana</s> demonstrates — with 'nor' etc. By 'street-balance-tip,' [meaning] by coincidence — that side of yours which is attached, O fortunate one, which even today, the side by which you passed beyond her. '<s>Rasa</s>-apprehension' — the apprehension of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) whose cause is mutual [attraction]. He strengthens the <s>rasa</s>-congruence of this content through the method of contrast (<s>vyatireka</s>) — with 'having touched you' etc. [Regarding] the verse with which the <s>Uddyota</s> was begun — 'the path of <s>dhvani</s> and of <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> has been shown' — the portion stating that 'by the path of <s>dhvani</s>, the <s>pratibhā</s>-quality of poets becomes infinite' has been explained — this he concludes with 'thus' etc. He then explains the portion regarding <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> — with '<s>guṇībhūta</s>' etc. The threefold <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested content) consists of <s>vastu</s> (content), <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornament), and <s>rasa</s> (sentiment); the subordination (<s>guṇībhāva</s>) of that [vyaṅgya] to the expressed — with respect to that, is the meaning.

children.text: atra tvamanavaratamarthāstyajasīti audāryalakṣaṇaṃ vastu dhvanyamānaṃ vācyasyopaskārakaṃ bālapriyā tribhedavyaṅgyāpekṣayetyetadvyācaṣṭe--triprabheda ityādi /
children.translated_text: [Locana:] Here, 'you constantly give away wealth' — the content with the characteristic of magnanimity (<s>audārya</s>), being suggested, is ancillary to the expressed — the <s>Bālapriyā</s> explains, with respect to the threefold <s>vyaṅgya</s>, with 'threefold' etc.
[Bālapriyā:] '<s>Bhāvahala</s>' etc.

[Sanskrit shadow (<s>chāyā</s>):] For the wealth of those who have taken shelter — being refugeless, whose sole champion [they seek] — exhausted in body from the wandering through the chain of protectors, overcome by fear —
not even a moment's rest has been given — 'this is fitting indeed!' //
[Bālapriyā:] '<s>Cāiaṇa</s>' etc.
[Vṛtti:] The <s>Locana</s> bestows novelty, even when the expressed meaning has been touched by an earlier poet.
For thus, an older <s>gāthā</s>: 'Their bodies unable to bear the exhaustion of wandering through the chain of protectors —
the wealth-seekers, pitiable householders, seem to be sleeping in their settled state.' //
— Thus the Sanskrit shadow. 'This is fitting indeed' — here, through rhetorical intonation (<s>kāku</s>), the meaning is: 'this is not fitting!' — that is the sense.

children.text: alaṅkāreṇa vyaṅgyena vācyopaskāre navatvaṃ yathā mamaiva-- vasantamattāliparamparopamāḥ kacāstavāsan kala rāgavṛddhaye /
children.translated_text: [Vṛtti:] Novelty through subordinated suggested <s>alaṅkāra</s> enriching the expressed — for example, by myself: 'Your locks, comparable in their chain of resemblances to bees maddened by spring, existed for the increase of passion, O beautiful one;
now gleaming with the dust-like pallor of the cremation-ground, how [can they conduce] even slightly to your dispassion?' //

children.text: atra hyākṣepeṇa vibhāvanayā ca dhvanyamānābhyāṃ vācyamupaskṛtamiti navatvaṃ satyapi purāṇārthayogitve /
children.translated_text: [Locana:] Here, through the suggested <s>ākṣepa</s> (objection/irony) and <s>vibhāvanā</s> (poetic fancy), the expressed meaning is enriched — thus there is novelty even when the expressed content has been attained by older [poets].
For thus, an older verse: 'Hunger, thirst, desire, envy,
and the great fear of death — these five increase in old age, even for the wise.' //
Thus.

children.text: vyaṅgyena rasena guṇībhūtena vācyopaskāreṇa navatvaṃ yathā mameva-- jarā neyaṃ mūrdhni dhruvamayamasau kālabhujagaḥ krudhāndhaḥ phūtkāraiḥ sphuṭagaralaphenān prakirati // //
children.translated_text: [Vṛtti:] Novelty through subordinated suggested <s>rasa</s> enriching the expressed — for example, by myself: 'This [decay] visible upon the head is surely not old age; rather this is that serpent of Time (<s>kālabhujaga</s>), blind with fury, who scatters with his hissings foam dense with manifest venom.' //

children.text: tadenaṃ saṃpaśyatyatha ca sukhitammanyahṛdayaḥ śivo pāyannecchan bata bata sudhīraḥ khalu janaḥ //
children.translated_text: 'And yet, seeing this, with a heart that considers itself happy, not desiring the remedy of <s>Śiva</s> [i.e., liberation] — oh! oh! Steadfast indeed is this person!' //
[Sanskrit shadow (<s>chāyā</s>):] Their bodies unable to bear the exhaustion of wandering through the chain of protectors, overcome by fear of loss of [their] lord's [favor] —
the wealth-seekers, pitiable householders, seem to be sleeping in their settled state. //

children.text:
iti chāyā /
arthaḥspaṣṭaḥ /
vasanteti /
kañcana mitraṃ prati kasyaciduktiḥ /
vasante vasantena vā mattā ye alayo bhṛṅgāstatparamparopamāḥ teṣāṃ paramparayā tulyāḥ atinīlasnigdhā iti yāvat /
tathābhūtāḥ kacā ityanena yauvanadaśā pradarśitā /
tava rāgasya vṛddhaye āsan kila /
śmaśānabhūbhāge ye parāgāḥ bhasmareṇavaste iva bhāsurāḥ śubhrāḥ jarayā śuklā iti yāvat /
ete kacāḥ /

children.translated_text: Because of being a stimulus (<s>uddīpaka</s>) for both passion (<s>rāga</s>) and dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>), the comparison with the respective [objects] has been employed.

children.text: tava manāgīṣadupi viraktaye vairāgyāya na bhavanti /
children.translated_text: 'Even slightly for your dispassion — for [your] detachment — they do not [conduce].'

children.text: tat tathaṃ vairāgyasya kāraṇe satyapi tadajananaṃ kuta ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'That is so' — the meaning is: even when the cause of dispassion exists, whence comes the non-arising of that [dispassion]?

children.text: anena pratyuta kāraṇābhāve 'pi kāma eva vardhanta ityarthasya kāmasya mahimā varṇayitumaśakya ityarthasya ca prakāśanādvibhāvanākṣepau vyajyete, tābhyāṃ ca vācyamupaskriyata ityāha--atra hītyādi // //
children.translated_text: By this, on the contrary: even in the absence of a cause, desire alone increases — the content [suggesting] the greatness of <s>kāma</s> (desire), i.e., the content 'the greatness of desire is impossible to describe' — by the manifestation of both, the suggested <s>vibhāvanā</s> (poetic fancy) and <s>ākṣepa</s> (ironic objection) are revealed, and by those two, the expressed meaning is enriched — thus he says: 'here indeed' etc.

— Thus the Sanskrit shadow. The meaning is clear. Regarding '<s>vasante</s>' etc. — this is someone's utterance addressed to a certain friend. Those bees (<s>ali</s>) who are maddened by spring or in spring — resemblances comparable to their chain, that is, similar to their succession — meaning: exceedingly dark and lustrous. 'Such locks' — by this, the state of youth is shown. 'They existed for the increase of your passion, certainly.' 'Gleaming like the dust (<s>parāga</s>), i.e., the ash-particles, of the cremation-ground' — meaning white, [i.e.] grey with age. 'These locks' —

children.text:
kṣuttṛṇṇetyādisamāhāradvandvaḥ /
jareti /
jarājīrṇa kañciduśyoktiḥ /
mūrdhni iyaṃ dṛśyamānā jarā na bhavati /
ayamasau kradhāndhaḥ /
kālabhujagaḥ kṛṇṇasarpaḥ /
atha ca antakarūpo bhujagaḥ /
phūtkāraiḥ sphuṭaṃ garalaṃ yeṣu tathābhūtān phenān prakirati varṣati /
iyaṃ na jarā, kintu śirasthakālabhujagābhivṛṣṭaḥ phenanikara
children.translated_text: [Bālapriyā:] '<s>Kṣuttṛṣṇā</s>' etc. — this is a <s>samāhāradvandva</s> compound. Regarding '<s>jarā</s>' etc. — this is an address [expressing pity] to someone worn out by old age. 'This [decay] visible upon the head is not old age.' 'This is that one — blind with fury.' '<s>Kālabhujaga</s>' (serpent of Time) — a black serpent. And also: a serpent in the form of death. 'He scatters' — that is, he rains down — foams that are of such a nature that the venom in them is manifest. 'This is not old age, but rather an outpouring of foam from the time-serpent stationed on the head' —
[<s>Kārikā</s>:] Through the support of <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) in this manner, and of <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion) as well,

children.text: na kāvyārtha-virāmo 'sti yadi syāt pratibhā-guṇaḥ // DhvK_4.6 //
children.translated_text: there is no end to the content of poetry — if the quality of <s>pratibhā</s> (creative imagination) exists. // DhvK 4.6 //
[Vṛtti recites:] Through the support of <s>dhvani</s> in this manner, and of <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> as well,
there is no end to the content of poetry — if the quality of <s>pratibhā</s> (creative imagination) exists. // 4.6 //

children.text:
satsvapi purātanakaviprabandheṣu yadi syātpratibhāguṇaḥ, tasmiṃstvasati na kiñcideva kavervastvasti /
bandhacchāyāpyarthadvayānurūpaśabdasanniveśo 'rthapratibhānābhāve kathamupapadyate /
anapekṣitārthaviśeṣākṣapapatanaina bandhacchāyeti nedaṃ nedīyaḥ sahṛdayānām /

evaṃ hi satyarthānapekṣacaturamadhuravacanaracanāyāmapi locanam atrādbhutena vyaṅgyena vācyamupaskṛtaṃ śāntarasapratipatyaṅgatvāccāru bhavatīti navatvaṃ satyapyasmin purāṇaśloke jarājīrṇaśarīrasya vairāgyaṃ yanna jāyate, tannunaṃ hṛdaye mṛtyurdṛḍhannāstīti niścayaḥ // 5 // // //
children.translated_text: [Locana:] For when this is so — even in the composition of words that is charming and sweet without regard for [specific] meaning, here the <s>adbhuta</s> (marvelous) suggested meaning enriches the expressed, and being an ancillary to the apprehension of the <s>śānta rasa</s> (tranquil sentiment), it becomes beautiful — thus there is novelty even given this older verse: 'When dispassion does not arise in one whose body is worn by old age, then surely the conviction "death does not exist" is firmly fixed in the heart.' // 5 //

[Vṛtti:] Even when compositions of earlier poets exist, if the quality of <s>pratibhā</s> exists — in its absence, the poet has no subject-matter whatsoever. Even poetic luster (<s>bandhacchāyā</s>) — the arrangement of words conforming to both [levels of] meaning — how can it be achieved in the absence of insight into meaning? Without attending to specific meaning, the mere falling of letters [on the page] does not constitute poetic luster — this is not what is dear to the hearts of connoisseurs.

children.text:
satsvapītyādi kārikāyā upaskāraḥ /
trīn pādān spaṣṭānmatvā turyaṃ pādaṃ vyākhyātuṃ paṭhati--yadīti /
vidyamāno hyasau pratibhāgaṇa uktarītyā bhūyān bhavati, na tvatyantāsannevetyarthaḥ /
tasminniti /
anantībhūte pratibhāguṇe /
na kiñcideveti /
sarva hi purāṇakavinaiva spṛṣṭamiti kimidānīṃ varṇyaṃ, yatra kavervarṇanāvyāpārassyāt /
nanu yadyapi varṇyamapūrvannāsti, tathāpyuktiparipākagumbhaghaṭanādyaparaparyāyabandhacchāyā navanavā bhaviṣyati /
yannaveśane kāvyāntarāṇāṃ saṃrambha ityāśaṅkyāha---bandhacchāyāpīti /
arthadvayaṃ guṇībhūtavyaṅgyaṃ pradhānabhūtaṃ vyaṅgyaṃ ca /
nedīya iti /
nikaṭataraṃ hṛdayānupraveśi na bhavatītyarthaḥ /
atra hetumāha--evaṃ hi satīti /
bālapriyā ityarthaḥ /
dhruvamityutprekṣāyām /
taditi janaḥ /
tadenān tathābhūtān phenān /
phenamiti tadenamiti vā pāṭhaḥ /
sampaśyati atha ca sukhitamanyahṛdayaḥ śivopāyaṃ necchaṃśca /
ataḥ sudhīraḥ khalvityanvayaḥ /
batetyadbhute /
jareti /
taditi tasmādityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: [Bālapriyā:] '<s>Jarā</s>' etc. '<s>Tat</s>' — means 'therefore.' 'The conviction that "death does not exist" is firmly fixed in the heart, surely' — this is the syntactic connection. // 5 //

[Locana:] 'Even when [compositions of earlier poets] exist' etc. — this is the elucidation of the <s>kārikā</s>. Considering the first three quarters to be clear, he reads the fourth quarter for the purpose of explanation — with 'if' etc. The meaning is: that <s>pratibhā</s>-quality, when present, becomes abundant in the manner described — but it is not entirely non-existent. 'In its absence' — when the <s>pratibhā</s>-quality has not become infinite. 'Not any whatsoever' — for everything has already been touched by earlier poets — so what now remains to be described, where the poet's descriptive activity could operate? [Objection:] Even if there is no unprecedented subject-matter, still the maturity of expression, the density of arrangement, and the like — constituting poetic luster (<s>bandhacchāyā</s>) in its ever-new forms — that will be always novel. On this account is the exertion for other poetry. Anticipating this, he says 'even poetic luster' etc. 'Both [levels of] meaning' — the <s>guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> and the primarily suggested (<s>pradhānabhūta vyaṅgya</s>). 'Close' (<s>nedīya</s>) — meaning: close to the heart, not deeply penetrating — this is the meaning. He states the reason for this — with 'for when this is so' etc. The <s>Bālapriyā</s> — this is the meaning. '<s>Dhruvam</s>' — in the expression of poetic fancy (<s>utprekṣā</s>). '<s>Tat</s>' — means 'that person.' '<s>Tad enān</s>' — 'those foams of such a nature.' The reading may be '<s>phenam</s>' or '<s>tad enam</s>.' 'Sees this, and yet with a heart that considers itself happy, not desiring the remedy of <s>Śiva</s>' — therefore '<s>sudhīraḥ khalu</s>' — this is the syntactic connection. '<s>Bata</s>' — [expresses] wonder.

children.text:
upaskāra iti /
satsvapītyādeḥ na kāvyārthavirāmo 'stītyanenānvaya iti bhāvaḥ /
yadītyāderbhāvaṃ vivṛṇoti--vidyamāna ityādi /
vṛttau 'bandhacchāye'tyasya vivaraṇam--'arthadvayānurūpaśabdasanniveśa'iti /
tadrūpā bandhacchāyetyarthaḥ /
'anapekṣite'tyādiśaṅkāgranthaḥ /
itīdaṃ sahṛdayānāṃ na nedīya iti sambandhaḥ /
punaśśaṅkate--'śabdārthayo'rityādi /
'kāvyatva' iti nimitte saptamī /
śabdārthayoḥ sahitayoḥ kāvyatvena hetunetyarthaḥ /
'tathāvidha' iti /
arthānapekṣacaturamadhuravacanaracana ityarthaḥ /
'kavyavyavasthe'ti /
kāvyavyapadeśa ityarthaḥ /
samādhatte---'pare'tyādi /
'tatkāvyatve'ti tatpadena paraḥ parāmṛśyate /
'kāvyasandarbhāṇām' iti /
tatkāvyatvavyavahāra ityanuṣajyate /
kāvyavyapadeśaḥ pravarteta /
śabdārthayoḥ sāhityena kāvyatve kathaṃ tathāvidhe viṣaye kāvyavyavastheti cet---paropanibaddhārthaviracane yathā tatkāvyatvavyavahārastathā tathāvidhānāṃ kāvyasandarbhāṇām /
na cārthānantyaṃ vyaṅgyārthāpekṣayaiva yāvadvācyārthāpekṣayāpīti pratipādayitumucyate--
children.translated_text:
[<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] 'Embellishment' — /
The purport is: the syntactic connection of 'even when [other meanings] exist' etc. is 'there is no cessation of poetic meaning.' /
She elucidates the purport of 'if' etc. — 'existing' etc. /
In the <s>Vṛtti</s>, the elaboration of 'the lustre of compositional structure' is: 'the arrangement of words conforming to both meanings.' /
The meaning is: a compositional lustre of that kind. /
'Unanticipated' etc. — this is the text of the objection. /
The connection is: this is not unfamiliar to connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdayas</s>). /
Again she raises a doubt — 'of word and meaning' etc. /
'Of poetry-hood (<s>kāvyatva</s>)' — the locative is in the sense of reason. /
The meaning is: by the reason of poetry-hood of word and meaning combined. /
'Of that kind' — the meaning is: composition of clever and sweet expression without regard for meaning. /
'Designation as poetry' — the meaning is: the appellation of poetry. /
She resolves — 'others' etc. /
'In its poetry-hood' — by the word 'that,' the other is referred to. /
'Of poetic compositions' — the connection is: such poetry-hood usage [applies]. /
The poetic designation would apply. /
If poetry-hood is established by the combination of word and meaning, how can there be poetic designation in such a domain? — if so, just as the usage of poetry-hood applies when the meaning is composed dependent on others, so too for such poetic compositions. /
And the infinity of meaning is to be established not only with reference to the suggested meaning but also with reference to the expressed meaning — to establish this, it is stated:
Through the varieties of condition, place, time, etc., there arises

children.text: ānantyam eva vācyasya śuddhasyāpi svabhāvataḥ // DhvK_4.7 //
children.translated_text: infinity itself of the expressed meaning, even in its pure form, by its very nature. // <s>DhvK</s> 4.7 //
Through the varieties of condition, place, time, etc., there arises
infinity itself of the expressed meaning, even in its pure form, by its very nature. // 7 //

children.text:
śuddhasyānapekṣitavyaṅgyasyāpi vācyasyānantyameva jāyate svabhāvataḥ /
svabhāvo hyayaṃ vācyānāṃ cetanānāmacetanānāṃ ca yadavasthābhedāddeśabhedātkālabhedātsvālakṣaṇyabhedāccānantatā bhavati /
taiśca tathāvyavasthitaiḥ sadbhiḥ prasiddhānekasvabhāvānusaraṇarūpayā svabhāvoktyāpi tāvadupanibadhyamānairniravadhiḥ locanam caturatvaṃ samāsasaṅghaṭanā /
madhuratvamapāruṣyam /
tathāvidhānāmiti /
apūrvabandhacchāyāyuktānāmapi paropanibaddhārthanibandhane parakṛtakāvyatvavyavahāra eva syādityarthasyāpūrvatvamāśrayaṇīyam /
kavanīyaṃ kāvyaṃ tasya bhāvaḥ kāvyatvaṃ, na tvayaṃ bhāvapratyayāntāt bhāvapratyaya iti śaṅkitavyam // 6 // // //
children.translated_text: 'That which is to be composed is <s>kāvya</s>; its state is <s>kāvyatva</s> (poetry-hood)' — but one should not suspect that this is a <s>bhāva</s>-suffix [derived] from a <s>bhāva</s>-suffixed [word]. // 6 // // //

[<s>Vṛtti</s>:] Even of the expressed meaning in its pure form — without regard for the suggested — infinity itself arises, by its very nature. /
For this is the nature of expressed meanings, both sentient and insentient: that through the variety of conditions, variety of place, variety of time, and variety of individual characteristics, there is infinity. /
And when those [meanings], being thus established, are composed even with the description of natural appearance (<s>svabhāvokti</s>) that follows their well-known manifold natures — [the poetry is] without limit. [<s>Locana</s>:] 'Cleverness' — compound-formation. /
'Sweetness' — absence of harshness. /
'Of that kind' — /
Even for those endowed with unprecedented compositional lustre, in composing meaning dependent on others, there would be only the usage of poetry-hood as attributed by others — therefore, the novelty of meaning should be resorted to.

children.text:
pratipādayitumiti /
prasaṅgāditi śeṣaḥ /
yadi vā vācyantābadvividhavyaṅgyopayogi tadeva cedanantaṃ tadbalādeva vyaṅgyānantyaṃ bhavatītyabhiprāyeṇedaṃ prakṛtamevocyate /
śuddhasyeti /
vyaṅgyaviṣayo yo vyāpāraḥ tatsparśaṃ vināpyānantyaṃ svarūpamātreṇaiva paścāttu tathā svarūpeṇānantaṃ sadvyaṅgyaṃ vyanaktīti bhāvaḥ /
na tu sarvathā tatra vyaṅgyaṃ nāstīti mantavyamātmabhūtatadrūpābhāve kāvyavyavahārahāneḥ; tathā codāharaṇeṣu rasadhvanessadbhāvo 'styeva /
ādigrahaṇaṃ vyācaṣṭe---svālakṣeyeti /
svarūpetyarthaḥ /
yathārūpasparśayostīvraikāvasthayorekadravyaniṣṭhayorekakālayośca /
bālapriyā syāditi śeṣaḥ /
locane bhāvaṃ vivṛṇoti---apūrvabandhetyādi /

children.translated_text: She shows the derivation of '<s>kāvyatva</s>' — 'that which is to be composed' etc. // 6 // // //

[<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] 'To establish' — /
'Incidentally' is the completion. /
Alternatively: since the expressed meaning, being of infinite variety, is useful for the manifold suggested meaning — and if that itself is infinite, then by its force alone the infinity of the suggested arises — with this intention, this is stated as directly relevant. /
'In its pure form' — /
The purport is: even without contact with the operation relating to the suggested domain, infinity belongs to the [expressed meaning] merely by its own nature; but subsequently, being infinite in that very nature, it manifests the suggested. /
But it should not be thought that the suggested is entirely absent there, since in the absence of [the suggested], which is its soul-form, the usage of 'poetry' would be lost. And in the examples too, the existence of <s>rasa-dhvani</s> is present indeed. /
She explains the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) — 'individual characteristics.' /
The meaning is: of form. /
As for instance, form and touch, in an intense single condition, residing in a single substance, and at a single time. /
[<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] The completion is: 'would be.' /
In the <s>Locana</s>, she elucidates the purport — 'unprecedented compositional' etc.

kārikāsthaṃ śuddhasyeti padamanyathāpratipattiparihārāya vyācaṣṭe--vyaṅgyetyādi /
vyāpāra iti /
vācyasyeti śeṣaḥ /
ātmeti /
ātmabhūtasya vyaṅgyasyābhāva ityarthaḥ /
hāniḥ abhāvaḥ /
nanu kīdṛśaṃ vyaṅgyaṃ tatra bhavatītyatrāha---tathācetyādi /
vṛttau'anapekṣitavyaṅgyasye'tyetadapyuktarītyā vyākhyeyam /
'taiśce'ti /
'taiḥ' vācyārthaiḥ /
'prathamameve'ti /
kāvyārthaḥ sampadyate /
tathā hyavasthābhedānnavatvaṃ yathā---bhagavatīpārvatī kumārasambhave 'sarvopamādravyasamuccayena' ityādibhiruktibhiḥ prathamameva parisamāpitarūpavarṇanāpi punarbhagavataḥ śambhorlocanagocaramāyāntī 'vasantapuṣpābharaṇaṃ vahantī' manmathopakaraṇabhūtena bhaṅgyantareṇopavarṇitā /
saiva ca punarnavodvāhasamaye prasādhyamānā 'tāṃ prāṅmukhīṃ tatra niveśya tanvīm' ityādyuktirbhirnavenaiva prakāreṇa nirūpitarūpasauṣṭhavā /
children.translated_text: And that very [<s>Pārvatī</s>], when being adorned at the time of the new wedding — through expressions like 'seating that slender one there, facing east' etc. — her beauty of form has been delineated in an entirely new manner.

children.text: na ca te tasya kaverekatraivāsakṛtkṛtā varṇanaprakārā apunaruktatvena vā navanavārthanirbharatvena vā pratibhāsante /
children.translated_text: And those modes of description, made more than once in the same [place] by that poet, shine forth either as non-repetitious or as brimming with ever-new meaning.

children.text: darśitameva caitadviṣamabāṇalīlāyām--- ṇa a tāṇa ghaḍai ohī ṇa a te dīsanti kaha vi punaruttā /
children.translated_text: And this has been demonstrated in the <s>Viṣamabāṇalīlā</s> — 'Neither does the limit of those form, nor do they appear in any way repetitious —

children.text: je vibbhamā piāṇaṃ atthā vā sukaivāṇīṇam // //
children.translated_text: the amorous gestures of the beloveds, or the meanings of good poets' words.' // //

[<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] She explains the word 'pure' in the <s>kārikā</s>, to prevent a misunderstanding — 'suggested' etc. /
'Operation' — /
The completion is: of the expressed meaning. /
'Soul' — /
The meaning is: the absence of the suggested which is of the nature of the soul. /
'Loss' — absence. /
Objection: what kind of suggested meaning exists there? — to this she says: 'and thus' etc. /
In the <s>Vṛtti</s>, 'without regard for the suggested' — this too should be explained in the manner stated. /
'With those' — /
'Those' — the expressed meanings. /
'At the very outset' — /
The poetic meaning is accomplished. /
For indeed, through the variety of conditions, novelty [arises] — for example: in the <s>Kumārasambhava</s>, though the description of the form of the goddess <s>Pārvatī</s> has been completed at first itself through expressions like 'with a collection of all comparison-materials' etc., still, when she comes within the sight of the blessed <s>Śambhu</s> (Śiva), she is described again in a different manner, as 'bearing the ornament of spring' — in a mode that serves as an instrument of <s>Manmatha</s> (Love).

children.text:
ayamaparaścāvasthābhedaprakāro yadacetanānāṃ sarveṣāṃ cetanaṃ dvitīyaṃ rūpamabhimānitvaprasiddhaṃ himavadgaṅgādīnām /
taccocitacetanabiṣayasvarūpayojanayopanibadhyamānamanyadeva sampadyate /
yathā kumārasambhava eva parvatasvarūpasya himavato varṇanaṃ, punaḥ saptarṣipriyoktiṣu cetanatassvarūpāpekṣayā pradarśitaṃ tadapūrvameva pratibhāti /
children.translated_text: For example, in the <s>Kumārasambhava</s> itself, the description of <s>Himavat</s> in its mountain-nature, and then its presentation from the sentient perspective in the affectionate speeches of the Seven Sages — that appears as entirely unprecedented.
And this is a well-known path among good poets.

children.text: idaṃ locanam na ca teṣāṃ ghaṭate 'vadhiḥ, na ca te dṛśyante kathamapi punaruktāḥ /
children.translated_text: This — [<s>Locana</s>:] 'Neither does the limit of those form, nor do they appear in any way repetitious —
the amorous gestures of the beloveds, or the meanings of good poets' words.' // //

[<s>Vṛtti</s>:] And this is another mode of variety through condition: that all inanimate entities have a second, sentient form, well-known through personification — as with <s>Himavat</s> (the Himālaya), <s>Gaṅgā</s>, etc. /
And that, when composed through a natural composition appropriate to the sentient subject, becomes something entirely different.

children.text:
cakārābhyāmativismayassūcyate /

priyāṇāmiti /

etadeva priyātvamucyate, yadāha-- bālapriyā prathamasarga ityarthaḥ /

ca prasthānaṃ kavivyutpattaye viṣamabāṇalīlāyāṃ saprapañcaṃ darśitam /
cetanānāṃ ca bālyādyavasthābhiranyatvaṃ satkavīnāṃ prasiddhameva /
cetanānāmavasthābhede 'pyavāntarāvasthābhedānnānātvam /
yathā kumārīṇāṃ kusumaśarabhinnahṛdayānāmanyāsāṃ ca /

children.translated_text: And even among those, between the modest and the immodest.

And of inanimate entities (<s>bhāvas</s>), each having its own nature differentiated by varieties of condition from inception onward — when composed one by one, [the description] attains infinity itself.

children.text: yathā--- haṃsānāṃ ninadeṣu yaiḥ kavalitairāsajyate kūjatā- manyaḥ ko 'pi kaṣāyakaṇṭhaluṭhanādāghargharo vibhramaḥ /
children.translated_text: For example — 'Those [lotus-stalks] which, swallowed by the calls of swans, cause some other throaty, rough, warbling charm to be produced from the astringent rolling in the throat —
those [stalks], now rivaling the tusk-sprouts of young, not-yet-hardened elephants, have emerged in the lotus-ponds — the first knots of lotus-root fibers.' // //

[<s>Locana</s>:] By the two '<s>ca</s>' particles, extreme wonder is indicated. /
'In any way' — /
The meaning is: even when examined with effort, repetition is not found — in sum. /
'Of the beloveds' — /
For a fortunate man with many beloveds, like the beloved of <s>Rādhā</s> [i.e., <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>], enjoying those various women in the felicity of love-play, does not see repetition in their amorous gestures — then /
this very quality of being beloved is what is spoken of, as he says — [<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] The meaning is: in the first <s>sarga</s> (canto). /
'Described' — /
The completion is: in the third <s>sarga</s>. /
'Whose beauty of form has been delineated' — /
The completion is: in the seventh <s>sarga</s>. /
'Those modes of description do not appear' — this is the connection. /
'Of that poet' — /
The meaning is: of that poet <s>Kālidāsa</s> as well. /
She shows the Sanskrit rendering (<s>chāyā</s>) of '<s>ṇaa</s>' etc. in the <s>Locana</s> — 'neither' etc. /
She elucidates 'the amorous gestures of beloveds do not appear in any way repetitious' — 'a man with many beloveds' etc. /
The connection is: 'then he does not see repetition in the amorous gestures.' /
'Then' — at the time of love-play. /
'As he says' — the completion is: the poet <s>Māgha</s>. /
And the path for the instruction of poets has been shown in detail in the <s>Viṣamabāṇalīlā</s>. /
And for sentient beings too, the otherness through conditions such as childhood etc. is well known among good poets. /
Even within the variety of conditions of sentient beings, there is manifoldness through sub-varieties of conditions. /
For instance, among maidens whose hearts have been pierced by the flower-arrow [of Love], and among others [in different states].

atra kecidācakṣarin---yathā sābhānyātmanā vastūni vācyatāṃ pratipadyante na viśeṣātmanā; tāni hi svayamanubhūtānāṃ sukhādīnāṃ tannimittānāṃ ca svarūpamanyatrāropayadbhiḥ svaparānubhūtarūpasāmānyamātrāśrayeṇopanibadhyante kavibhiḥ /

etadeva viśadayati---pratyakṣetyādi /
ata eva sa prakāraviśeṣo yairadyatanairabhinavatvena pratīyate teṣāmabhimāna mātrameva bhaṇitakṛtaṃ vaicitryamātramatrāstīti /
tatrocyate--yattūktaṃ sāmānyamātrāśrayeṇa kāvyapravṛttistasya ca parimitatvena prāgeva gocarīkṛtatvānnāsti navatvaṃ kāvyapravṛttistasya ca parimitatvena prāgeva gocarīkṛtatvānnāsti navatvaṃ kāvyavastūnāmiti, tadayuktam; yato yadi sāmānyamātramāśritya kāvyaṃ pravartate kiṅkṛtastarhi mahākavinibadhyamānānāṃ kāvyarthānāmatiśayaḥ /
vālmikivyatiriktasyānyasya kavivyapadeśa eva vā sāmānyavyatiriktasyānyasya kāvyārthasyabhāvāt, sāmānyasya cādikavinaiva pradarśitatvāt /
uktivaicitryānnaiṣa doṣa iti cet--kimidumuktivaicitryam? uktirhi vācyaviśeṣapratipādi vacanam /

children.translated_text: When there is variety in expression (<s>ukti</s>), how can there not be variety in the expressed content (<s>vācya</s>)?
Because [linguistic] activity proceeds from the inseparable connection of the expressed (<s>vācya</s>) and the expressive medium (<s>vācaka</s>).

children.text: locanam pratyakṣadarśane 'pi hi--- śabdāssaṃketitaṃ prāhurvyavahārāya sa sbhṛtaḥ /
children.translated_text: [<s>Locana</s>:] For even in the case of direct perception — 'Words designate what is conventionally agreed upon (<s>saṃketita</s>), employed for the sake of practical usage (<s>vyavahāra</s>).'

children.text: tadā svalakṣaṇaṃ nāsti saṅketastena tatra naḥ // //
children.translated_text: 'Then there is no <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular characteristic); hence for us there is no convention (<s>saṅketa</s>) regarding that.'

Thus this method should be followed in other cases as well. [<s>Locana</s> (commentary):] 'That which attains novelty at every moment — that alone is the form of <s>ramaṇīyatā</s> (aesthetic charm).' By 'of the beloved ones' (<s>priyāṇām</s>) — the particular <s>vibhrama</s> (amorous play) of the beloved women, which flows continuously throughout <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), is seen as ever-new. For it is not learned from elsewhere like the construction of a fire-altar (<s>agnicayana</s>), whereby it would fall into repetition (<s>punaruktā</s>) through similarity to that [model]. Rather, it is merely the blossoming of the sprout of <s>Madana</s> (the god of love), arising spontaneously from nature — hence its ever-newness. Likewise, the meaning of poetry (<s>kāvyārtha</s>) is an outflow of one's own innate <s>pratibhā</s> (creative genius), not dependent on instruction from others — this is the purport. [<s>Bālapriyā</s> (sub-commentary):] He states the meaning conveyed by 'the <s>vibhramas</s> (amorous plays) of the beloved ones' — beginning with 'of the beloved ones' etc. 'For not' etc. — that particular <s>vibhrama</s>. The meaning is: it is not learned in the way that <s>agnicayana</s> (fire-altar construction) is learned from others. 'Whereby' — the meaning is: by virtue of being learned from others. 'That' — the meaning is: the particular <s>vibhrama</s>. 'Ever-newness' — the word 'of that' is to be supplied. He elucidates the topic at hand, namely 'the meanings of good poets' — beginning with 'likewise' (<s>tadvat</s>). 'Likewise' — the meaning is: comparable to that, it becomes ever-new. In the <s>Vṛtti</s> (gloss): 'when we consider the nature of inanimate things' — 'the description of <s>Himavat</s> (the Himālaya)' is to be connected. 'That has been shown' — the meaning is: that has been described. 'Even when there is no difference in state' — the meaning is: even when there is no difference in bodily states such as childhood etc. 'Internal' — the meaning is: mental. Regarding 'of the <s>haṃsas</s> (swans)' — '<s>kabalitaiḥ</s>' means 'consumed.' By which, in the cries of the cooing swans, a certain hoarseness from the scraping of the throat with astringent [food] — some other <s>vibhrama</s> (charm) is produced — and so forth by analogy. He explains in the <s>Locana</s> the word <s>tāvat</s> ('at least') in the phrase 'even that which exists as it is, when composed [in poetry]' — beginning with 'but in the later time' etc. The diversity of inanimate things arises from difference of place — this much at least. As is well known regarding winds moving in various directions and regions, and also regarding water, flowers, and the like. Even among sentient beings — humans, animals, birds, and so on — nurtured in villages, forests, waters, etc. — a great mutual difference is indeed observed. And when that is discerningly composed as appropriate, it achieves exactly that [novelty]. For instance — even among humans alone, differentiated by direction and region, who can reach the end of the varied particularities in their dealings and activities — especially those of women? And all of that is composed by good poets according to their <s>pratibhā</s> (creative inspiration). And diversity arises from difference of time — as in the case of inanimate things like the directions, sky, water, etc. due to seasonal variation. Among sentient beings too, states like longing (<s>autsukyā</s>) etc. residing in particular times are well known indeed. And the composition of things throughout the entire world according to their distinctive characteristics (<s>svālakṣaṇya</s>) is well established. And even that which exists as it is, when composed [in poetry], produces the very infinitude of poetic meaning. Here some say: things enter the domain of the expressed (<s>vācya</s>) only in their generic form (<s>sāmānyātman</s>), not in their particular form (<s>viśeṣātman</s>); for they are composed by poets who project the generic form of their own and others' experienced pleasures and their causes onto other [subjects], relying only on the commonality of form experienced by self and others. For poets do not perceive the past, future, and present with their unfamiliar particularities directly as <s>yogins</s> do; and that commonality of experience to be conveyed, being shared by all recipients and being limited, has already been traversed by the ancients — hence it cannot be the domain of [novelty]. [<s>Locana</s>:] Regarding '<s>tāvat</s>' — 'but in the later time, through contact with <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested meaning), it attains the highest variety; but in that much [i.e., at the literal level] alone, that variety exists by its very nature' — this is the purport of the word <s>tāvat</s>. 'And of their causes' — of seasons, garlands, and the like, this is implied. The commonality of what is experienced by oneself and by others — that alone, devoid of further particulars — relying on just that. 'For not by them' — means by the poets. And this is said to express utter impossibility. [<s>Bālapriyā</s>:] She explains 'experienced by self and others' — beginning with 'experienced by oneself' etc. The explanation of the meaning of the word <s>mātra</s> ('mere') is: 'devoid of further particulars.' In the <s>Vṛtti</s>: 'the particular nature of the unfamiliar etc.' — the meaning is: the true nature of unfamiliar things etc. 'And this has been said' — this is the connection. 'For not' etc. — the meaning is: and [this is] a statement [to that effect]. 'For the purpose of expressing utter impossibility' — the meaning is: for the purpose of conveying the utter impossibility, namely the non-existence of the possibility of presenting things in their particular form. She makes this very point clear — beginning with 'direct perception' etc. Therefore, the variety proclaimed by those modern [poets] as being novel is merely their own conceit — there is only a semblance of variety here.
